- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-12 (built on branch `lazylist-perf`): **A lazy list's cell is one object of three words,
  filled in place by the one function that evaluates it.** `LazyList[+T]` holds `pending` (the
  evaluating function until it has run, a constant trapping function while it runs, then `None`),
  `first` and `rest`; an empty cell is one whose `rest` is itself, and a cell evaluated as another
  list's first cell whose rest would be itself points at that other cell instead (the same element,
  then itself again), so a list that is its own tail still repeats. Making a cell allocates the cell
  and the function that evaluates it, and evaluating it allocates only the cells after it and the
  elements; a cell is read with a test of `pending` and no lock, since a lazy list is not sendable.
  To keep the element and the rest in a covariant class, the core library gains the intrinsic
  **`field_unset`**: `private var x: T = fieldUnset()` is a field the constructor leaves as the zero
  bytes the object was made with (not yet a value, as an array's spare capacity is not), which the
  class's own code writes before reading it; such a field must be a `private var` with its type
  written, is not a position for the class's variance (it is written only with values computed for
  that instance), and the intrinsic is the core library's alone; called anywhere but as a field's
  initializer it traps (`a field is read before it is set`). Measured at `-O2` (`LazyList.from(0)`
  and the stages named, then `take(n)`, the cost per element; time under a loaded machine, user
  time): bytes kept per evaluated cell 256 → 48 (resident growth per held cell 304 → 96); bytes
  allocated per element of `from`, `map`, `filter` or `take` 304 in 7 objects → 96 in 2, and of
  `#::` 544 in 13 → 192 in 4 (two cells, each with its function); time per element of
  `from.take` 0.118 → 0.035 µs, `map` 0.18 → 0.058, `filter` 0.24 → 0.079, `#::` 0.18 → 0.065, the
  4000th prime by the sieve 4.8 → 1.7 s; at `-O0` `from.take` 0.16 → 0.06 µs. `lazy_list_deep` runs
  a million cells again. WHY: each cell was a `LazyList` object, a progress object, the closure of
  its `lazy val`, a box and a closure to drop the pending function, the function itself, and a
  tuple for the evaluated element and rest, with a lock-taking `lazy val` read on every access; the
  element and rest belong in the cell, which only a field left unset can hold, since a covariant
  class may not otherwise keep a `var` of its parameter and a field must otherwise be given a value
  when the object is made. The counts are pinned by `lazy_list_cell_tests.sysl`, which reads them
  from the code each maker compiles to; no runtime allocation counter was added, since the code is
  where an allocation is decided and the test holds however a run is timed. ALTERNATIVES: a cheaper
  `lazy val` (no closure per object) with the tuple kept (three objects per element, still a lock
  per read); `Option[T]` for the element (allocates a `Some` for every scalar element); a separate
  evaluated node per cell (two objects); an annotation exempting a field from variance, with an
  initial value supplied some other way (two mechanisms where one does); a runtime allocation
  counter exposed to programs (a hook in every allocation, for a check the code already answers).
  Review with the user: `field_unset` is a new escape from the variance and initialization rules,
  though only the core library may use it.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-12 (built on branch `train-c-fix`): **Proposed (branch `train-c-fix`): an argument that cannot be checked before an overload is chosen
  is tried against each candidate.** Where a lambda's body, checked with its result left open (the
  rule `map-flatmap` added for `flatMap`'s `Iterable`/`Option` overloads), reports an error, or a
  generic function named as a value cannot be checked without the parameter's type, the argument is
  checked against each remaining candidate with nothing reported and nothing it settles kept; when
  exactly one candidate takes it, that one is chosen and the argument checked against it. Otherwise
  the argument is checked as before and reports what is wrong. A lambda whose body never returns
  (`x -> fail(…)`) fits every candidate, and the first declared is chosen (an option's own `flatMap`
  on an option). WHY: with one `flatMap`, `v.flatMap(n -> if … then aList else aVector)` and
  `xs.flatMap(identity)` checked against its `Iterable[U]`; the second overload took that expected
  type away, so the branches no longer joined and `identity` could not be instantiated — a call that
  compiled stopped compiling because an overload was added. ALTERNATIVES: always prefer the
  `Iterable` overload (a rule naming library types, and wrong for `[Some(1)].flatMap(identity)`);
  report such calls as ambiguous and ask for a type (breaks code that worked); join the branches to
  their least common supertype without an expected type (changes `if` typing everywhere). A trial
  checks the argument once per candidate, which costs only where candidates disagree.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-12 (built on branch `train-c-fix`): **Proposed (branch `train-c-fix`): a class with a field left unset by `field_unset` is made only by

  constructors in general (a language feature, reviewed separately for `Time`/`Zoned`); a constructor

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-12 (built on branch `defer-use`): **resource cleanup is a block-scoped `defer` statement,
  and the library's resources are each an `io.Close`**
  ([defer](/spec/operators-and-control-flow/#defer), [`Close`](/spec/system-library/#close)).
  - **`defer stmt`** (or `defer` and an indented block) runs the statement when control leaves the
    block it is written in: at the block's end, `return`, `?`'s failure arm, `break` and `continue`.
    The reached ones run last first; one not reached never runs; names are read when it runs, and a
    block's, `return`'s or `break`'s value is computed before. No `return`, `?`, or `break`/`continue`
    of an outer loop may leave a deferred statement. It is a statement of a block only: as a value, a
    one-line branch or in a class body it is refused. While one waits, nothing is in tail position,
    so `@tailrec` refuses a self-call there. `defer` becomes a keyword (one test function named
    `defer` was renamed).
  - **A trap and `process.exit` run no deferred statement.** There is no unwinding; files and
    connections left open are closed by the collector's finalizers.
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `defer-on-cancel`): **a cancelled
    thread runs its deferred statements**, innermost first, as at any other way out of their blocks,
    wherever its cancellation stops it (a wait, a safepoint poll), and then its frames are dropped
    as before. A thread running a scope stops first at that scope: the scope body's deferred
    statements run, the scope cancels its threads and waits for them (each running its own), then the
    functions around the scope run theirs. **A deferred statement runs to its end once begun**: the
    thread's cancellation does not stop it inside one (its own waits are not cancellation points
    while it runs, as while a lock is held), and one that comes meanwhile stops the thread at its next
    cancellation point after; one that traps stops the program, as any trap. **A cancelled wait on a
    mutex's condition stops the thread holding the lock again**, so a `with` body's deferred
    statements run under it and `with`'s own `defer` lets it go; the library's internal conditions
    still stop without the lock, as their code expects. `Pool`'s putting back what a cancelled call
    held is now a `defer`.
    *Why*: cancellation stops a thread at a known point, a wait or a poll, in a consistent state,
    unlike a trap. Without it no library or package can clean up after a cancelled task: found
    writing a PostgreSQL client, where a cancelled query must send a CancelRequest, a cancelled
    `transaction(f)` must roll back, and a pool lease or a `Mutex.with` must be given back.
    *Alternatives weighed*: a public `onCancel(cleanup)(body)` in `avin.threads` (a second mechanism
    beside `defer`, and lambdas again, with the `return`/`?`/`break` problem `defer` was chosen to
    avoid); leaving it (no cleanup at all after a cancellation); running a deferred statement with
    cancellation live (a cleanup that waits could itself be cut off half done).
  - **Each deferred statement is its closure, put on the thread's list where the `defer` is
    reached** (`lower.sysl`'s `Defer`, `runtime/avin/rt/defers.sysl`): every way out of the block runs
    the block's own from the list, newest first, and a cancellation runs every one reached since the
    cancellation point it returns to before it drops their frames; a trap in an actor's turn drops
    the ones it passes unrun. A function that defers nothing never touches the list. The checker
    checks the statement as a lambda of no parameters that no jump may leave, so a `var` it reads is
    shared as a captured one is. *Why*: the cancellation unwinds by returning to the cancellation
    point past every frame between, so what those frames deferred must be reachable from the thread
    itself; a list costs a closure and two runtime calls per deferred statement and nothing anywhere
    else. *Alternatives weighed*: emitting each deferred statement inline at every exit, as before,
    and a landing pad per function that defers (a `setjmp` in every such call, with the locals it
    reads unreliable after the return); a frame-local record pointing at a compiled cleanup function
    (no allocation, but a new kind of stack object for the collector and the code generator).
    **Review with the user**: deferred statements now allocate a closure where they capture
    anything, a cost on the ordinary path (`Mutex.with` among them); a later pass could emit them
    inline again where no cancellation point can be reached between the `defer` and its block's end.
  - **`trait io.Close { close() -> Result[unit, IoError] }`**, closing twice answering `Ok`:
    `fs.File` (unchanged), the new `fs.TempDir` from `fs.tempDir(prefix)` (`close` removes the tree),
    every `net.ByteStream`, `TcpListener` and `UnixListener` (their `close` now answers `Ok(())`
    rather than `unit`; `TlsStream`'s answers the failure to send its close notice), and
    `process.Child` (new `close`: kill if not seen to end, then wait; a detached child is let be).
    `Mutex.with`/`update` release their lock through `defer`.
  - *Why*: the paths that leak are early `return`, `?` and `break`, and only a construct the
    compiler places at every exit covers them; a library `use(r)(body)` puts the body in a lambda,
    where a `return`, a `?` of the enclosing function, a `break` or a `continue` cannot be written at
    all. Block scope (not function scope) gives back each loop turn's resource before the next and
    needs no run-time state; reading names at the exit needs no storage. The syntax and the rules
    are Sysl's own `defer`, so the two languages read alike. `Close` answers a `Result` because a
    flush, a removal and a wait can fail, and `File.close` already did.
  - *Alternatives weighed*: a library `use(resource)(body)` over a `Close` trait (cannot leave the
    enclosing function from the body; nests one lambda per resource); function-scoped `defer`
    evaluating its arguments where written (holds every turn's resource until the function returns,
    needs a run-time list); `try`/`finally` (a second block structure for one need); running deferred
    statements on a trap (unwinding through a broken state); a `Close` whose `close` answers `unit`
    (would drop `File.close`'s flush error and a `TempDir`'s removal error); `use x = e` binding sugar
    over `defer x.close()` (left for later; `defer` covers it in one more line).
  - **Review with the user**: whether discarding a `close`'s `Result` in `defer` deserves a warning;
    whether `use x = e` sugar is wanted.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-12 (built on branch `numeric`): **`Numeric`, the numbers' bound.** A core trait
  `Numeric: Add, Sub, Mul, Div, Rem, Neg, Ord, Display, Debug` declaring `toReal -> real`; `Integer`
  now requires it (`trait Integer: Numeric`), so every width meets it through one
  `impl[T: Integer] Numeric for T`, and `real` has its own impl. Why: a mean, a clamp or a running
  total over `int` and `real` alike had no bound to name (`[T: Add]` cannot reach a `real`, and
  `Integer` excludes `real`); taking every operator the integers and `real` share (`Div` and `Rem`
  included, though their meaning differs: integer division truncates and traps on zero) gives the
  most generic code, and `zero`/`one` are already `Add`'s and `Mul`'s. Alternatives: only
  `Add & Sub & Mul & Ord` (the audit's sketch), which leaves `/` out of generic numeric code; a
  `Numeric` that also offered `fromInt`/`T(n)` construction, left out since `zero`/`one` cover the
  identities and a conversion from integers is lossy at narrow widths; a separate `Fractional` for
  `real`, not needed while `real` is the one non-integer. **Review with the user**: whether `Div`
  and `Rem` belong in it.

  type that implements the required traits and `toReal` is a number (a rational type is the

  reach every `[T: Numeric]` function. Alternative: closed like `Integer`, which would keep `toReal`
  meaningful only for built-ins at the cost of every user number.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-12 (built on branch `numeric`): **`average` totals as `real` and traps when empty.**
  `average` on a collection of `Numeric` elements is a `real` mean summed through `toReal`, so
  integers whose sum overflows their type still average (beyond 2⁵³ the total rounds);
  `average` traps on an empty collection as `max` and `min` do, and `averageOption` answers
  `None`. Alternatives: summing in `T` and converting once (exact for small integers, but traps
  where the mean is representable); NaN for an empty collection (silent, unlike `max`); only
  `averageOption`. `sum`, `product`, `min` and `max` were already generic over `Add`, `Mul` and `Ord`
  and are left as they were rather than duplicated on `Numeric`.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-12 (built on branch `numeric`): **`real(x)` on a `Numeric` parameter is refused, naming
  `.toReal`.** A call converts only a type parameter bounded by `Integer`; a `T: Numeric` converts
  with its own method. Why: a conversion call on a type parameter is lowered per instance by the
  compiler for integers only, while `toReal` is an ordinary trait method a program's own number
  implements. Alternative: lower `real(x)` to `x.toReal` for a `Numeric` parameter, more uniform

  `path-helpers`). Proposed: `fs.walk(root) -> Result[Vector[Entry], IoError]`, depth first, a
  directory before its contents, each directory's names in code-point order (as `listDir`), the root
  itself left out; `Entry(path, relative, depth, isDir, isLink, error)`. A link is listed and never
  followed (`isDir` false for it), the root is followed when it is a link, and a directory that cannot

  problem deep in a tree spoiling the rest. Alternatives weighed: a lazy iterator of
  `Result[Entry, IoError]` with pruning (sysl's shape: cheaper on a huge tree, but every item needs
  its own `?` and the order is the file system's); failing the whole walk at the first error; skipping

  characters, and a byte `?` would match a third of `文`; component-wise matching makes `glob`'s answers

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `argparse`): **`avin.cli`: a declared parser read by name** (branch `argparse`). Proposed: the standard
  library's argument parser is a `Parser` value built by chained declarations (`flag`, `string`,
  `int`, `real`, `choice`, `positional`, `positionals`, each with named `short`, `help`, `default`,
  `required`, `repeated`, `value`), and `parse(args)` answers `Result[Args, ArgsError]`; values are
  asked for by name and type (`a.int("top")`, `a.strings("file")`), and asking for an undeclared
  name or the wrong type traps. `parseOrExit` covers the usual `main`: help or version to standard
  output and status 0, a mistake to standard error with the usage line and status 2. Why: it needs
  no language feature, a program reads in the order its help does, and every mistake a user can
  make is a value with a sentence naming what they wrote. Alternatives weighed: deriving a parser
  from a `data` type's fields (`data Options(...) derives Args`), which checks names at compile time
  but needs a derivation and a way to attach help, short letters and defaults to fields; a
  getopt-style loop the program drives, which is what `wc` hand-rolled; one getter returning
  `Option` for everything, which makes every read a `match`. Review with the user: whether a
  derived form is wanted on top of this one.
  The rules it settles, each the common command-line convention: `--name=value` and `--name value`
  alike; bundled letters (`-lw`, `-n5`, `-lwn5`); an option's value is the next argument whatever
  it starts with (`--top -1`); `-` alone and the empty argument are positional; `--` ends the
  options; options and arguments interleave; a single option given twice keeps the last (so an
  alias's option can be overridden), a `repeated` one keeps all, and a flag is counted (`-vvv`).
  Every parser has `--help`/`-h`, and `--version` where it has a version, unless the program
  declares that name or letter itself; each acts where it stands, left to right. An option with no
  `default` reads as its type's zero (`""`, `0`, `0.0`) and `given(name)` tells whether it was on
  the command line; the help shows a default only where it is not that zero, since a default
  parameter cannot tell an explicit zero from an omitted one. Every option has a long name (the
  name `Args` looks it up by); positional arguments are strings. The reasons read ``unknown option
  `--x` ``, `` `--count` needs an int, not `abc` `` and `` `--scale` needs a number, not `x` ``
  (a user of the program knows "number" better than "real"). Alternatives weighed: refusing an
  option given twice (catches typos, breaks overriding an alias); refusing a value that starts with
  `-` unless it is a number; typed positional arguments, left out until a program needs one;
  `Option`-typed defaults (`default = Some(3)`), exact but noisy at every declaration.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (built on branch `cli-subcommands`): **`avin.cli`
  commands are parsers of their own.** `Parser.command(sub)` adds the command `sub.name`, whose
  options and arguments `sub` declares and whose help line is `sub.about`; a command may have
  commands (`git remote add`). The first positional argument names the command and every argument
  after it is the command's, so the program's options come before the command word and the
  command's after it (`todo --file t.txt add -p high milk`); a parser with commands takes no
  positional arguments, and declaring both traps. `Args.command` is the command's name (empty where
  the parser has none) and `Args.commandArgs` the command's own `Args`. While a command reads its
  arguments its parser is named after the program and the command, so its usage line, help and
  messages say `todo add`. Every parser with commands has the command `help` (`todo help add`,
  `todo help remote add`) unless the program declares one of that name, as with `--help`; `todo add
  --help` is the command's own. No command is ``missing command; the commands are `add`, …``; an
  unknown one is ``unknown command `lst`; did you mean `list`?``, the suggestion being the nearest
  name within two edits (fewer than the word's characters), else the one name the word begins,
  else the list of commands. WHY: a sub-parser is the value a program already knows how to build,
  so a command needs no new kind of declaration, and nesting comes free; reading only the program's
  options before the word is the convention every tool with commands follows, and keeps a
  command's options free to reuse the program's names. Alternatives weighed:
  `command(name, help, sub)` (repeats what `sub` already holds); a dispatch table of functions
  (`command(sub, run)`) that `parse` would call, which hides control flow and fixes a return type
  on every command; options of the program accepted after the command word too (ambiguous where
  both declare a name); a missing command printing the help instead of a mistake; matching
  commands by unique prefix outright (`todo l` running `list`), which turns a later command into a
  breaking change. Review with the user: whether a missing command should show the help (git's
  way) rather than be a mistake.
  **A mistake is reportable without ending the program.** `ArgsError.Invalid` gains `program`
  (the name of the parser that found it, `todo add`) and `hint` (``Run `todo add --help` for the
  options.``, ``Run `todo --help` for the commands.``, or `help` where `--help` is the program's
  own, or empty), so `Invalid(reason, usage, program, hint)`; `ArgsError.report` is the whole
  text `parseOrExit` writes, every line ending in a newline, and `exitCode` its status (0 for the
  help or the version, 2 for a mistake). A shell or script runner calls `parse`, writes
  `e.report` and reads the next line; `message` and the `Display` stay the reason alone, so an
  `ArgsError` passed on with `?` still reads as one sentence. WHY: the error must carry the
  failing command's name, since only it knows it; a parser method `report(e)` would name the
  top program for a command's mistake. Alternatives weighed: keeping `Invalid(reason, usage)` and
  folding the name into `usage` (changes what the field means); making the `Display` the whole
  report (a multi-line display breaks error chaining). Review with the user: the two new fields
  change `Invalid`'s shape, so a program matching `Invalid(reason, usage)` must add `_, _`.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `small-papercuts`): **one family of case names, `toUpper` and `toLower`, for
  `char` and `string` alike.** `string.toUpperCase` and `toLowerCase` are renamed to `toUpper` and
  `toLower`, the names `char` already had, across the library, its tests, the corpus, the scripts
  and the spec; `"a".toUpperCase` is refused with ``string has no field `toUpperCase`; a string
  maps its case with `toUpper` and `toLower`, as a `char` does``. WHY: one name for one operation
  on both types, and the shorter one, which conflicts with nothing on either type. There is no
  deprecation mechanism to keep the old names as aliases, so the old names are gone and the error
  names the new ones. ALTERNATIVES: rename `char`'s to `toUpperCase` (longer, and `isUpper`/`isLower`
  on `char` would then disagree with it); keep both names on `string` as plain aliases (two names for
  one method forever, with no way to retire one). Review with the user: it breaks source using the
  old names (marshal, tui and typing-practice use them), so their call sites change in the release
  that carries it.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `small-papercuts`): **`avin` takes its options before or after the program.**
  The program is the first argument that is neither an option nor an option's value, wherever it
  stands before `run`'s `--`; for `avin test`, only an existing path is the program and any other
  word is the filter, as before. `avin run -O2 main.avin`, `avin run main.avin -O2`,
  `avin -O2 main.avin` and `avin build -o out -O0 main.avin` are all accepted, and only what follows
  `--` reaches the program. A first argument that is any option (not only `-O0`, `-O2` or `--`) now
  means `avin run`, which checks the options itself. WHY: the audit's `avin run -O2 file.avin`
  printed the whole usage; the order of avin's own options carries no meaning, and `--` already
  separates the program's arguments. ALTERNATIVES: options after the program only, with an error
  saying so (keeps a rule nobody needs); treating words after the program as its arguments without
  `--` (makes `avin run main.avin -O2` pass `-O2` to the program, which surprises in the other
  direction). One exception, from branch `script-deps` (below): `avin <file> ...`, with no command
  word, for a file whose first line begins `#!`, gives every argument after the file to the program,
  since that is how a `#!/usr/bin/env avin` line runs it as a command.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `small-papercuts`): **`Result.toOption` beside `ok`, and `StringWriter` is
  `Display`.** `toOption` answers exactly what `ok` does, under the name `Either` and the
  collections use; `ok` stays. `StringWriter` implements `Display` (its `text`, padded to a field's
  width, as a string) and `toString()` returns its `text`. WHY: the names people reach for first,
  and a writer that interpolates as what it holds. ALTERNATIVES: renaming `ok` to `toOption`
  (breaks callers for no gain; `ok`/`err` read as a pair); a `StringWriter` with `toString()` only
  (it would still show as its type's name in `s"$w"`).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `small-papercuts`): **`t._1` on a tuple names the part to write.** A member
  `_` followed by decimal digits asked of a tuple adds ``; a tuple's parts are numbered from 0, so
  write `.n-1` `` when `1 <= n <=` its arity, and ``; a tuple's parts are numbered from 0 and read as
  `.0` to `.k` `` otherwise (`_0`, a part beyond the arity, a number too large to read). WHY: the
  `_1` spelling is what readers of other notations write first, and `_n` meaning part `n - 1` is the
  likely intent. ALTERNATIVES: accepting `_1` as a second spelling (two ways to write one thing).

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `build-dir`): **`avin run` and `avin test` build into the user's cache
  directory, not into `.avin/` beside the program.** A program's executables and its instance cache
  go to `build/<name>-<key>/` in the toolchain's cache (`~/Library/Caches/avin/<version>/` on macOS,
  `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/avin/<version>/` or `~/.cache/avin/<version>/` elsewhere, or `AVIN_CACHE`), where
  `<name>` is the program's directory's or file's name and `<key>` twelve hex digits of a SHA-256 of
  its absolute, canonical path. `.avin/build/` beside the program is used only on a machine with no
  cache directory (no `AVIN_CACHE`, `HOME` or `XDG_CACHE_HOME`; the runtime's archives then go to the
  temporary directory, which is cleared under a long-lived cache). `avin build` and `-o` are
  unchanged. The new `avin clean [<program>]` removes the program's directory and any `.avin/build/`
  beside it (on the fallback, a program of one file's entries only, and `.avin/` once empty);
  `avin clean --all` removes the whole `build/` of this version and nothing else of the cache, and on
  the fallback means the current program's. `avin new` writes `/<name>` (the executable `avin build`
  leaves at the root) and `.avin/` into an application's `.gitignore`, `.avin/` alone into a
  library's. Why: a one-file script run from anywhere left an `.avin/` next to it; Sysl keeps its
  builds and run cache in the machine cache directory keyed by version and target and uses a
  project's `.sysl/` only where there is none, and Avin already keeps its fetched packages, runtime
  archives and shims there, so a build cache beside the source was the one exception. Keying by path
  keeps two worktrees of one repository apart (each has its own sources), and the version in the
  path keeps one compiler's entries from another's. The executables and records are still published
  by rename and the instance cache is lock-free as before, so two builds of one program at once stay
  safe. Alternatives weighed: keep `.avin/` beside projects and move only one-file programs (two
  rules to explain, and a repository still grows a directory to ignore); key by the program's content
  rather than its path (every edit would start a new cache, and nothing would ever trim the old);
  `--all` removing the whole `avin/<version>` (it would also drop fetched packages, which a build
  then fetches again over the network); a lock around a program's cache (the content-addressed,
  rename-published entries need none). Review with the user: whether a cache of a deleted project
  should ever be trimmed on its own (answered by the cache's limit: least recently used first, see
  the Proposed entries of branch `cache-trim`).

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `variant-test-open`): **A variant with fields named alone in a pattern
  tests for the variant and binds none of its fields.** `o.status is Shipped`, `Shipped -> …` in a
  `match` arm, `Status.Shipped` qualified, `Some(Shipped)` nested and `f(Shipped) = …` in a clause
  all mean `Shipped(_, _)`, with the variant's own number of `_`; coverage and unreachable arms
  treat it as that pattern. `Shipped()`, written with parentheses, is still matched against the
  fields by number and refused for a variant that has some. Why: the commonest test of a variant
  asks only which one it is, and counting `_`s to say so is noise that changes whenever a field is
  added; the previous error suggested `Shipped(fields)`, which is not Avin, and the bare name could
  mean nothing else, since a variant in scope is never a binding. One rule for every place a
  pattern goes, because `x is P` takes exactly the patterns a `match` arm takes. Alternatives: only
  in `is` (two pattern languages, and a `match` arm refactored from an `if … is` would break);
  keeping the error and suggesting `Shipped(_, _)` with the right number of `_` (valid, but the
  test still has to change with the fields). Review with the user: a reader may take `Shipped`
  for a variant without fields.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `variant-test-open`): **`open`, `abstract` and `override` where they
  mean nothing are one error each, and the declaration then parses as written.** Before a method:
  "a method takes no `open`: every public method of an `open` or `abstract` class, and every
  method of a trait, may be overridden already; remove `open`", and for `abstract` that a method
  declared without a body is abstract already; before a field, that a field cannot be overridden
  or is abstract by having no value; before a top-level function, that it belongs to no class or
  overrides nothing; before `trait`, `data` and `object`, why each takes none; `override class`,
  that a class replaces nothing and extends with `: Base`. Why: the words were read as names, so
  `open sound() -> string` reported `open` and `string` as undefined and then every override of
  `sound` as overriding nothing. The spec settles that every public method of an open class may be
  overridden, so methods have no `open` to accept. Alternatives: accepting `open` on a method as a
  harmless no-op (two spellings of one meaning); a method-level `open` with classes' methods
  final by default (a language change the settled rules do not ask for). `open(…)`, `open = …`
  and a method named `open` keep their meaning: the word is a modifier only before a name or a
  declaration keyword.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `bigint`): **`BigInt` is a class of the core module `avin`, written in Avin, its
  magnitude in limbs of nine decimal digits held in `long`s.** It is visible with no import, as
  `BitSet` is; its limbs are a `FrozenArray[long]`, a type no program can name, so its constructor
  cannot be called with a malformed magnitude from outside the library, and the value is immutable
  and sendable. Multiplication is schoolbook and division is long division with a normalized
  divisor, both quadratic. *Why*: base 10^9 makes decimal text, by far the commonest, a limb at a
  time in both directions, and keeps a limb product plus a carry inside a `long` with no wrapping
  arithmetic; living in `avin` lets it reuse the integer formatter's private layout code, so `%d`
  and its flags behave exactly as for `long`. *Alternatives*: binding Sysl's `sysl.math.bigint`
  through a handle (faster, but its behaviour, text forms and traps would be Sysl's to change, and
  the library is meant to be Avin); base 2^32 limbs (cheaper bit operations, which `BigInt` does not
  have yet, but every decimal conversion becomes a division per nine digits and products need
  wrapping or 128-bit arithmetic); a module `avin.math` needing an import (keeps the core namespace
  smaller); Karatsuba multiplication (not needed at the sizes programs meet so far). Review with the
  user: whether `BigInt` should be in the core namespace, and whether it should gain the bitwise
  operators and shifts.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `bigint`): **`BigInt`'s API mirrors the integer methods: `abs`, `sign`, `pow`,
  `gcd`, `lcm`, `floorDiv`, `floorMod`, `toRadix(r)`, plus `isZero`, `divRem`, `toLong`/`toInt`
  that trap and `toLongOption`/`toIntOption` that answer `None`.** Made by `BigInt(n)` from any
  integer width (a non-generic `apply(n: long)` beside the generic one, so a literal as large as a
  `long` is accepted), `BigInt(text)`/`BigInt(text, radix)` that trap on bad text as `toLong` does
  (`For input string: "…"`), and `BigInt.parse(text[, radix])` answering `Option`. A zero divisor
  traps with `division by zero`. *Why*: one vocabulary for whole numbers, so code moves between
  `long` and `BigInt` by changing a type; the trapping and `Option` pairs follow `string.toLong` /
  `toLongOption`. *Alternatives*: `toString(radix)` instead of `toRadix` (the integer types already
  chose `toRadix`); only `Option` conversions (forces `.get` at every call that knows the value
  fits); a `string.toBigInt` extension (adds to every string a method for one type).

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `bigint`): **the integer format conversions `%d`, `%i`, `%x`, `%X`, `%o` and
  `%b` take a `BigInt`, and `%s` refuses it as it refuses every number.** The checker names the core
  library's `BigInt` beside the integer widths and `byte`. *Why*: a whole number is formatted as one,
  with grouping, signs, zero padding and bases; refusing `%s` keeps the rule that a number's
  conversion says how its digits are laid out. *Alternatives*: a trait (say `WholeNumber`) a type
  implements to be taken by the integer conversions (general, but a new trait and a display
  contract for one type); accepting `BigInt` under `%s` (inconsistent with every other number).
  Review with the user: whether a trait should open the integer conversions to other types.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `bigint`): **a type's static member is called on its name even where the type
  has a companion object.** `Cup.zero()` with `object Cup` declared reported "`Cup` has no member
  `zero`" (and `Period.zero()` the same), since the name was read as the object. Now `Name.member`
  is the companion's where the companion declares a member of that name, and otherwise the type's
  static member where it has one, for classes and data types, written with type arguments or not,
  called or named as a function value. *Why*: the spec calls a static member on the type's name, and
  a companion is where a type keeps its factories, so a type with both is the ordinary case
  (`BigInt.zero()` beside `BigInt.apply`). *Alternatives*: refusing a static member and a
  companion on one type (rules out the common case); the type's static member winning over the
  companion's member of the same name (makes a companion unable to shadow it deliberately).

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `json-package`): **the corpus programs that test the compiler with

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `json-package`): **a trap inside a package is placed in the package's
  source**, as before for any module that is not the core library: `j("absent")` now reports

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `script-deps`): **A program of one file names its dependencies in a header of
  comment lines at its top**: the line `// avin.hocon`, then `//` lines whose text after the `//` is
  exactly a manifest's `dependencies` block, ending at the first line that is not a `//` comment
  ([packages](/spec/packages/#programs-of-one-file)). Why: domain libraries are packages (JSON, CSV),
  and a script must reach them without becoming a directory with a manifest; reusing the manifest's
  own HOCON means one syntax, one parser and one set of errors, shown at the header's line in the
  file. Being comments, the header needs no change to the lexer, the parser, the formatter or the
  IntelliJ plugin, and a file with one is still Avin to every tool. `// avin.hocon` reads as "this
  file's manifest", and the editor grammar colours the block as embedded HOCON. Alternatives weighed:
  a `---` front-matter fence (a second lexical form every tool must learn, and a file no older
  compiler reads); a declaration in the language, `dependencies { … }` or an annotation on the file
  (dependencies are the build's business, not the program's, and the checker would have to ignore
  it); one `@dep("github.com/…@1.0")` comment per dependency (a second syntax for what a manifest
  already says, without `path`, `rev`, `member` or features); a block comment (Avin has none).
  Review with the user: the marker's spelling.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `script-deps`): **The header holds `dependencies` only, and is at the top or
  refused.** `workspace = true` and `optional` are refused (no workspace, no features of its own);
  `package`, `features`, `sysl-dependencies` and `c-libraries` are refused at the key, a program that
  needs them being a package. It begins on the first line, or the second after a `#!` line; a
  `// avin.hocon` line anywhere else is an error, because a header silently not read is a missing
  dependency reported as an unknown module. Alternatives weighed: allowing `sysl-dependencies` and
  `c-libraries` (each works through the same resolution, and may be added when a script needs one);
  allowing other comments or blank lines before it (a header that moves is harder to find, and the
  rule "first line" is one a reader can check at a glance).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `script-deps`): **A header in a file of a package, or of a program of many files,
  is refused at the header**, rather than merged with the manifest or passed over. Why: two places
  naming a package's dependencies would disagree, and passing it over hides a mistake; a directory
  program has no manifest, and the way to give it dependencies is to make it a package. Only the
  package's own files are checked; a dependency's files are not.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `script-deps`): **A program of one file's sum file is beside it, named after it**:
  `tool.avin.sum`, written and checked as `avin.sum` is, absent when nothing is fetched, rewritten by
  `avin tidy tool.avin`. A program of one file is **not vendored**: `avin vendor` refuses it, and
  `avin add` (which edits a manifest) refuses it too. Why: the sum file is where a manifest's is,
  beside what names the dependencies, and naming it after the file lets several scripts share a
  directory. A `vendor/` beside the file would be shared by every script in the directory, and
  vendoring one would remove the others' packages. Alternatives weighed: no lock at all, trusting

  directory (scripts would add and `tidy` would remove each other's lines); the hashes written into
  the header (the build would rewrite the user's source); a `vendor/<file>/` per script. Review with
  the user: whether a script's sum file is wanted, or is clutter next to a one-file tool.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `script-deps`): **A
  first line beginning `#!` is not Avin**, in every file, and the line is written
  `#!/usr/bin/env avin`. **`avin <file> ...` (the form a `#!` line runs, with no command word)
  for a file whose first line begins `#!` gives every argument after the file to the program**, so
  `./tool.avin -O0 x` passes `-O0` and `x`. Every other form keeps the command line's rule:
  `avin run tool.avin -O0 -- x` and `avin -O2 tool.avin -- x` take the options as avin's and pass
  only what follows `--`. Why: `./tool.avin a b` runs `avin ./tool.avin a b` through the `#!` line,
  and without the rule the program's arguments would need a `--` that a command's caller cannot know
  to write; while a person typing `avin run` is using avin, and its options mean the same wherever
  they stand. Alternatives weighed: every argument after any `#!` file the program's, `avin run`
  included (the branch's first form; it made `avin run tool.avin -O0` mean something different for
  one kind of file); `#!/usr/bin/env -S avin run` as the line (needs `env -S`, and runs through
  `avin run`, where the options are avin's); `#!` lines needing `avin run --` (env passes the file
  after the `--`, so it would be an argument, not the program); taking options before the first
  non-option and the rest as the program's (`./tool -O0` would still be eaten). Review with the
  user: the argument rule, which makes `-O0` after a `#!` file the program's when run as a command.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `fmt-pack`): **`avin fmt` fills a broken literal of short, simple items, as many to a line as fit** (branch
  `fmt-pack`). A sequence literal `[…]` or set literal `{…}` (brackets not after an operand, so no
  index or type arguments) whose every item is a number, a character, a plain string, `true`,
  `false` or a name, a number with a sign against it included, and no item wider than 32
  characters, is broken where any list would be (past 120 characters, or written with a line
  break after its opening bracket and before its closing one), but its items are then laid out
  `, `-separated, as many to a line as fit in the 120 columns, two columns in, a trailing comma
  kept after the last. Any other item (a call, a lambda, a tuple, a nested literal, an
  interpolated string, a `key: value` entry) keeps the one-item-per-line layout, and a comment
  among the items keeps the lines as written, as everywhere inside brackets. Arguments of a call
  are never filled. The result is idempotent: a filled literal is broken after its opening bracket,
  so formatting it again fills it the same way. WHY: a generated table (tui's `width_table.avin`,
  about 640 pairs of code points) became ~1,280 lines of one number each; filled, it is 111 lines
  and reads as a table. ALTERNATIVES: keep a source that is one per line one per line (leaves the
  table unreadable, and a table that has been through `fmt` once could never recover); fill any
  list of one-token items, call arguments included (a call's arguments are each a meaning, and
  one per line shows them); fill short tuples `(a, b)` too (more rules for the reader of the style
  to learn; a table of pairs is written flat, as tui's is); align items into columns (wider diffs
  for one changed entry, and no gain for numbers of one width). Review with the user: the 32-
  character limit, and whether a short list deliberately written one per line should stay so.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `discarded-result`): **A dropped `Result` or `Future` is an error, and
  `_ = e` drops one on purpose** ([errors](/spec/errors/#a-result-is-not-dropped)). A value of
  either type is reported where it is thrown away: a block's statement, the last line of a function
  or lambda yielding `unit`, a branch of an `if` without `else` or of an `if`/`match` written as a
  statement, a loop's body. `_ = e` evaluates `e` and keeps nothing. A deferred statement is exempt,
  and so is an expression the checker reads only for its own errors after the form around it failed.
  The standard library's call sites were each handled or marked `_ =` (a socket or pipe closed once
  its exchange is over, a temporary directory removed, a signal to a program that may have ended).
  - *Why*: `fs.writeText("/nonexistent/x", "hi")` as a statement compiled and failed silently (gap
    audit C8). An error, not a warning: Avin has no warnings channel, every diagnostic is an error,
    and a warning shown only sometimes is the one that is missed (as for unreachable match arms).
    `_ = e` is the spelling a reader already knows from destructuring, where `_` drops a part. A
    deferred statement is exempt because it runs while its block is being left, where no `?` or
    `return` can carry a failure anywhere, and `defer f.close()` is the form `defer` exists for. A
    `Future` is included because dropping one loses its answer the same way.
  - *Alternatives weighed*: a warning (no channel to carry it); a `@mustUse` annotation on types or
    functions (more general, but a new attribute for two types, and a library author could forget
    it); `Result` only (a dropped `Future[Result[…]]` loses the failure just as surely); reporting
    a dropped `Result` in `defer` too, which would make `defer _ = f.close()` the idiom (noise on the
    one form `defer` is for); `val _ = e` as the only discard (it already works, but reads as a
    declaration).
  - **Review with the user**: whether `defer` should stay exempt (decisions above left "whether
    discarding a `close`'s `Result` in `defer` deserves a warning" open), and whether a lambda yielding
    `unit` should be held to the rule (it is, so `xs.foreach(f -> fs.remove(f))` is an error).

  integer literal where such a type is expected is `T.fromInteger(literal)`, the literal typed as a

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-12 (built on branch `library-version`): **the standard library carries the compiler's version, and
  the compiler refuses a library of any other.** `library/library.hocon`'s `package.version` is
  stamped by `scripts/release.sh` in the same commit as `const Version` and `compiler/sysl.hocon`,
  and a compiler checks it against its own before it compiles anything: `check`, `build`, `run`,
  `test` and `lsp` print one error naming both versions and the library's path, and nothing else.
  A library with no version, or a `library.hocon` that is missing or unreadable, is refused the
  same way. The rule is an **exact match**. A compiler built between releases carries the last
  release's version, and so does the library in its own checkout, so a development build matches
  its own tree; only a library from another release, through `AVIN_ROOT` or an install, differs.
  Why: a library of another version fails as dozens of errors inside `library/avin/*.avin`, which
  points a reader at the library rather than at the mismatch. Alternatives weighed: a dev compiler
  accepting a library from the same commit (needs a commit id stamped into both and a build step
  that keeps them in step, to answer a case the exact rule already passes); "the library is newer
  than the compiler" (a newer library declares what an older compiler cannot check, which is the
  failure being fixed). Review with the user: whether a pre-release suffix should be accepted in the
  library's stamp; manifests accept three numbers only, as `sysl.hocon`'s version does.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-13 (built on branch `fmt-two-space`):
  **`avin fmt` keeps a function's clauses together.** No blank line goes between a function's
  signature and its first clause or between two of its clauses, at the top level, in a class, an
  object, a trait or a block alike, and blank lines the source wrote there are dropped, around
  any comments between the clauses too (the comments stay). A clause is recognised as the parser
  recognises one: the name of the signature or clause before it at its level, an argument list,
  then `=`, a guard or an indented block of guards; the signature is a line naming the function
  with typed parameters, no `=` and no indented body. The function counts as one declaration, so
  the blank line between it and a different declaration before or after it stays as before, and a
  blank line inside a clause's body is the body's own and stays. In a literate file, blank lines
  beside prose are the document's and are kept even between clauses. Why: a function written as
  clauses is one declaration and the preferred form for a function that matches on its
  parameters; a blank line before a multi-line clause, which the rule for top-level declarations
  put there, makes it read as several declarations. Alternatives weighed: keeping the blank lines
  the source wrote and only not adding any (a file would read differently by who wrote it, and the
  formatter is meant to settle exactly this); a blank line between clauses only around a

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `api-websocket`): **What a WebSocket
  does by itself**: a ping is answered with a pong as it arrives and a pong is passed over; a
  fragmented message is put back together, control frames between its fragments answered; the size
  limit is checked against a frame's declared length before its payload is read, so an oversized
  message is refused without being buffered (`1009`); text is checked to be UTF-8 once the message
  is whole (`1007`), and so is a close reason; a frame breaking the protocol (`1002`) — a client's
  frame not masked or a server's masked, a reserved bit, an unknown opcode, a fragmented or long
  control frame, a continuation with nothing to continue or a new message inside one, a close of
  one byte or with a code no endpoint may send, a 64-bit length with its top bit set — fails the
  connection: the close frame is sent and the connection closed at once. A close from the other end
  is answered with its code (none for none, heard as `1005`) and the connection closed; this end's
  `close` waits `closeTimeout` for the answer. A session returning with its WebSocket open closes it
  with `1000`; a server stopping closes it with `1001` at its next receive (the wait being through
  `idle`) or send; a peer going without a close is `Closed(1006, …)`. A frame's length need not be
  in its fewest bytes, though this end writes it so; every message is sent as one frame; a client
  masks each frame with four bytes from `SecureRandom`. Why: these are RFC 6455's rules where it
  gives them, and where it leaves a choice (validating UTF-8 at the end rather than as fragments
  arrive, accepting a longer-than-needed length) the simpler one that still refuses what it must.
  Alternatives weighed: surfacing pings and pongs as messages (every session would answer them by
  hand); validating UTF-8 per fragment (fails a bad message sooner, at more code). **Review with the
  user:** a `WebSocket` belongs to one thread, as its stream does (a TLS stream checks its owner), so
  a session that must send what another thread produces while also receiving polls with
  `receive(limit)`; a `select`-like receive over a channel, or a sendable sending half, would be the
  next step if a program needs one.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `lazy-local`): **A local `lazy val`, in a block, is the value of a
  cell made where it is declared**, the core library's private `LazyCell[T]`, holding the value, its
  state word and the closure computing it, so a read is that cell's lazy field read: once on the
  first read, under the same protocol as a field's between threads, with the same trap for a read
  made while it is being computed. The choices the request left open:
  - *Closures share it.* A closure capturing the name captures the cell, so a first read inside
    the closure computes it for the enclosing scope too, and the reverse; it outlives its block. A
    declaration in a loop body makes a new cell on every pass. *Alternatives*: copying the value
    into the closure at capture (would force it where the closure is made, defeating the point);
    one cell per declaration site (wrong for loops and recursion).
  - *The initializer sees the locals as they are at the first read*, a captured `var` included,
    since it is a lambda run then; fields see their object at the first read in the same way.
    *Alternative*: snapshotting the locals at the declaration (would need a copy of every captured
    `var`, and differs from what a lambda written in the same place does).
  - *Across threads, sendable where its type is and its initializer would be.* A `@sendable`
    closure (a thread's body, a future's) may capture a local `lazy val` only where the value's
    type is sendable and every local and parameter the initializer captures passes the rules that
    closure is held to, a `var` refused, through each lazy value the initializer reads in turn; what
    the initializer reaches is held to the module-level state rule too. *Why*: the initializer may
    run on whichever thread reads first, so it is code the closure carries; a field's initializer
    captures only its object, which the object's own sendability covers. *Alternatives*: refusing
    every capture of a lazy local by a `@sendable` closure (simpler, but refuses the plain case of
    a sendable value computed from sendable `val`s); checking the value's type alone (unsound: an
    initializer capturing a `Buffer` or a `var` would run on another thread).
  - *A self-read follows the other lazy values*: today it traps at run time, ``avin: trap: `x` is
    read while it is being initialized``, as a field's and a module-level value's do, and a lazy
    list may refer to itself through its cells. The sound-initialization design (`### lazy val` in
    declarations) makes a read the initializer's own code reaches a compile error; a local is held
    to it in the same way when that is built, and its run tests `lazy_local_self_direct` (a direct
    read, which becomes a reject test) and `lazy_local_self` (a read through a closure the
    initializer calls, which stays a trap) say which side each falls on. A trap in the initializer
    stops the program as any trap does.
  - *The type must be known where it is declared*: an initializer whose type is not settled there
    (one reading only its own value) is refused with "cannot infer the type of `x`", as a field's
    is, rather than settled by later uses as a plain `val`'s may be. An initializer that never
    finishes gives the type `Nothing`. A mismatch with a declared type is reported as "the
    initializer of `x` yields …".
  - *One name per declaration*: `lazy val (a, b) = …` and `lazy val a, b = …` are refused ("take
    the value apart where it is read"), as is a `lazy val` without an initializer; an assignment, a
    compound assignment and a step are refused as for a module-level `lazy val`.
  - *Cost*: a declaration allocates the cell and the initializer's closure, both kept until the cell
    is unreachable. *Alternative weighed*: storing the value, state and closure in boxed locals
    without an object (saves one allocation but needs a layout of its own in the lowering and a
    separate sendability rule); clearing the closure after the first read (frees its captures early,
    but fields keep theirs, and a race-free clear needs another store on the hot path).
  Review with the user: the cross-thread rule (the more permissive of the two sound choices).

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `sync-kit`): **A `WaitGroup` counts work and has no `spawn`.** `add`,
  `done`, `wait`, a timed `waitFor` and `pending`; a count below zero traps. Why: a scope already
  starts threads and waits for them structurally, so a spawning wait group would be a second way to
  do what `scope` does; what a wait group adds is counting work finished by threads started
  elsewhere (an executor, an actor, another scope) or by no thread at all. Alternatives weighed:
  `wg.spawn(body)` starting and counting a thread (duplicates `Scope.spawn`, and an unscoped spawn
  escapes cancellation); answering a negative count by clamping at zero (hides a double `done`).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `sync-kit`): **A `Semaphore` has a capacity, and a release beyond it
  traps.** `Semaphore(permits, capacity = permits)`; negative permits, a capacity below one or more
  permits than the capacity trap too. Permits belong to no thread, and waiters are not queued (one
  arriving as a permit comes back may take it first). Why: an over-release is the same bug as a
  wait group's double `done`, a permit given back that nobody took, and a trap finds it where it
  happens; the separate capacity keeps the signalling use (`Semaphore(0, capacity = 1)`) that an
  "at most the initial permits" rule would forbid. Alternatives weighed: an unbounded count (a
  silent over-release grows the limit for good); permits owned by the thread that took them (rules
  out a permit taken by one thread and given back by another, which hand-offs need); a FIFO queue
  of waiters (a cancelled waiter would have to take its place back, for a fairness the condition's
  oldest-first wake mostly gives already). Review with the user: trap or ignore an over-release.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `sync-kit`): **`withPermit` and a `RwLock`'s read give back what they
  hold when a cancellation stops their body; a `RwLock`'s write runs to its end; a trap in any of
  them stops the program.** The share is taken under the library's lock and held in a region in
  doubt from that moment until it is given back (the runtime's new `lock_release_holding` and
  `cancel_guarded_held`), so no cancellation can come between taking it and the body. A read body
  or a permit's body runs at a cancellation point of its own inside that region, so a cancelled scope stops
  a long download inside `withPermit` at once and the permit goes back, while a trap there, even in
  an actor, stops the program as one under a lock does, since recovering the actor's turn would
  leave the share held for ever. A write body is also uncancellable, as a `Mutex`'s body is, since
  stopping it could leave the value half changed. Why: a semaphore guards no value, and a reader
  changes nothing, so nothing is left in doubt by stopping them; a writer does change the value.
  Alternatives weighed: every body uncancellable, as a mutex's (a scope's cancellation would wait
  for every permit holder's whole body); every body cancellable (a write could leave the value
  torn); a trap in an actor's body failing only the actor (needs a give-back chain run by the
  actor's recovery, which the runtime does not have).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `sync-kit`): **A `RwLock` lets writers in first, and lets in the readers
  a write kept waiting before the next writer.** A reader that arrives while a writer waits waits
  behind it; when a write ends, every reader then waiting is admitted ahead of the writers waiting.
  Why: writers do not starve under overlapping readers, and readers do not starve under back-to-back
  writers, with no tuning. Alternatives weighed: pure writer preference (readers starve while
  writers keep coming); reader preference (writers starve); a strict FIFO of both (serialises
  readers that could share). Review with the user: a read body is trusted only to read; nothing
  stops it changing a mutable value other readers share, which races with them (a race is not
  undefined behaviour in Avin, but the type system does not rule it out here as it does elsewhere).
  A read-only view of a value would close it and is a language feature, not a library one.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `sync-kit`): **A `Barrier`'s action runs under its lock, and a party
  cancelled while waiting withdraws.** The last arrival runs the action holding the barrier's lock,
  so the action is uncancellable and one that waits on its own barrier traps as a lock taken twice
  does; `wait` answers whether the caller arrived last. A cancelled waiter takes its arrival back
  (it is not counted for the round), through the runtime's settling condition wait, which answers a
  cancellation with the lock held again rather than stopping at once. Why: a scope cancelled
  mid-round leaves the barrier as if the stopped parties had never come, ready for new ones.
  Alternatives weighed: a cancelled party staying counted (the round could trip with a party
  missing); "breaking" the barrier for every party (a state each `wait` would have to answer);
  running the action outside the lock (waiting on its own barrier would then deadlock instead of
  trapping).

- Settled by the user 2026-11-14 (built on branch `contextual-keywords`, from the user's decision of 2026-11-14 that
  `data` keeps its spelling and becomes contextual): **the words that begin a top-level declaration
  are keywords only there, before the name they declare, and ordinary names everywhere else**:
  `data`, `class`, `object`, `trait`, `impl`, `import` and `module` join `type`, `opaque`, `export`,
  `derive`, `actor` and `machine`, and `open` and `abstract` are keywords only before `class`. So
  `val data = readFile(p)`, a field `class`, a method `object()`, a parameter `import`, a named
  argument `module = 2`, a type parameter, a variant, a module named `data` and `r.type` are all
  legal, and `data(x: int)` at the top level declares a function called `data`. **The reserved
  words stay**: `as`, `is`, `match`, `then`, `else`, `elif`, `do`, `yield` and `derives`, because each
  follows a complete operand on its line (`x as T`, `if c then a`, `Base(x) derives Eq`), where a
  name is an infix call; `if`, `while`, `for`, `loop`, `defer`, `return`, `break`, `continue`, `val`,
  `var` and `def`, because each begins a statement or a declaration inside a block, where a line may
  equally be an expression starting with a name (`loop` and an indented block would read as a call
  of `loop` with a trailing block; `return (x)` as a call); `private`, `static` and `override`,
  because they begin a member of a class body, where a line may be a statement, and `private + (o:
  T)` would be both a method named by a symbol and an expression on a value; `true`, `false`,
  `self` and `super`, which are values. `end` keeps its rule (a keyword only before a name), and
  `not` and `with` theirs. Why: the test is whether the keyword's every position can be told from a
  name's by the next token alone. A top-level line holds only declarations, never a statement, so a
  declaration word followed by a name can mean nothing else, and none of these words begins
  anything inside a block or a class body. Alternatives weighed: renaming `data` (the user kept the
  spelling); making every word contextual by look-ahead over whole lines (`loop`, `return` and the
  modifiers would each need a rule of their own that a reader cannot see at a glance); keeping
  `class` and `object` reserved as the most declaration-like (they are common field names, and
  nothing about them is less decidable than `data`). The user
  settled 2026-11-14 that `private`, `static` and `override` stay reserved: a modifier used as a
  variable name would read strangely.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-14 (built on branch `hkt-7`): **a trait for types whose
  members never write `Self` bounds constructors too**
  ([generics](/spec/generics/#constructor-traits)). A trait with parameters, no static member, no
  member naming `Self` beyond the receiver, and requiring only such traits (`Foldable[A]`, any
  `Countable[A]` of a program's own) is a trait for types everywhere it is one, and also a bound of
  a constructor parameter of its arity: `impl Foldable for Option` makes each `Option[T]` a
  `Foldable[T]`, so `Option` is a constructor for `[F[_]: Foldable]`, and a constructor trait may
  require it at its own parameters (`trait Traverse[A]: Functor[A], Foldable[A]`). A type conforms
  as a constructor only where a conformance states the trait's parameters as its own parameters,
  so `impl Foldable[int] for Ints` makes no constructor; a type whose parameter is bounded is one
  only for a hole promising that bound (`TreeSet` for `F[_: Ord]`), as for a constructor trait; a
  trait naming `Self` otherwise or declaring a static member bounds types only, and one writing
  `Self[X]` stays a constructor trait, never a type. Why: `Foldable`'s method mentions no `Self`,
  so what it promises of an `F[X]` is exactly what the type conformance promises of that type; one
  trait serves both uses, generic code over constructors reads the conformances the collections
  already have, and nothing new is needed at run time (each instance's call is the ordinary call on
  its type). Alternatives weighed: a constructor trait requiring a trait for types at its holes (a
  constraint on every application `Self[A]`, a second notion with its own rules, where the dual
  reading needs none); giving `Foldable` a method that writes `Self` (an artificial member, and it
  would stop `Foldable[int]` being a type). This supersedes the Proposed "a constructor trait
  requires only constructor traits" (branch `hkt-3`) for traits that bound constructors.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `api-pool`): **a resource pool is
  `avin.threads.Pool[T, E]`, lending through a body** ([pools](/spec/threads/#pools)). `use(f)`
  and `lease(f)` lend a resource for the call of `f` and always take it back, answering
  `Result[R, PoolError[E]]`; there is no `acquire`/`release` pair. Why: the scope of the body is
  what makes "always returned" true by construction, on a return, a cancellation inside it, and a
  trap (which stops the program); a resource handed out by `acquire` comes back only if every path
  remembers to give it back. It sits in `avin.threads` beside the semaphore it resembles, built on
  the same lock and cancellation machinery; the executor's private worker pool, which was also
  called `Pool`, is renamed `WorkerPool`. Alternatives weighed: an `acquire()` answering a lease to
  `release()` by hand (an actor holding a connection across messages would want it; it can be added
  beside the body form later); a module of its own (`avin.pool`), which would need the threads
  module's private machinery made public. **Review with the user:** whether an explicit
  acquire/release form is wanted for resources held across an actor's messages.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `api-pool`): **a pool's resources
  are isolated rather than sendable.** A `Pool` is sendable whatever `T` is, as a `Mutex` is:
  `create`, `validate` and `destroy` are `@sendable`, so a resource is made from sendable values
  alone, and `use`'s and `lease`'s bodies are `@isolating` and give back a sendable `R`, so the
  resource never leaves the call it is lent to. Why: the resources worth pooling are mutable
  (a connection's buffers and state), and a program's mutable class cannot promise `Sendable` (the
  `@trusted_sendable` mark is the standard library's), so a pool that asked `T: Sendable` could not
  hold the database client it exists for. The cost: a body may not capture a mutable value from
  around it, and two mutable resources cannot be used in one nested body (`db.use(c ->
  cache.use(r -> … c …))` is refused, since the inner body captures `c`). Alternatives weighed:
  `T: Sendable` (sound, and too narrow, as above); unrestricted bodies (a resource kept past its
  call would be used by two threads at once). **Review with the user:** the nested-body
  restriction, which a borrow form the language does not have would lift.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `api-pool`): **a pool's waiters
  are served first come, first served, by direct hand-off.** A resource given back goes straight
  to the call that has waited longest, and so does the place a destroyed resource or a failed make
  gives up; a new call queues behind any waiter even when it comes just as a resource is given
  back, so no call is overtaken. Idle resources are lent most recently used first, so the oldest
  expire under `idleTimeout`. Why: fairness the brief asks for, and an `AcquireTimedOut` under
  load then means the pool is too small rather than unlucky. Alternatives weighed: waking any
  waiter and letting it race (the semaphore's way; cheaper, and unfair); oldest idle first (keeps
  every connection warm, and none ever expires on a quiet server).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `api-pool`): **every function a
  pool runs for a call runs where a trap cannot be contained.** A trap inside `f`, `create`,
  `validate` or `destroy` stops the program even in an actor, as one inside `withPermit` does.
  Why: an actor that survived the trap would leave the pool counting a resource or a place that is
  never given back, shrinking it for good. `f` and `create` stay cancellable; `destroy` runs to its
  end. Alternatives weighed: containing the trap and leaking the place (a pool that slowly loses
  capacity in a long-running server). **Review with the user:** a server whose handlers are actors
  may prefer the handler's failure to the program's.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `api-pool`): **idle resources
  expire when the pool is next used, not on a timer of their own.** A call looking for a resource,
  and `evictIdle()`, destroy those idle longer than `idleTimeout`, keeping `minIdle`; `minIdle`
  also sets what `warm()` makes, and is not kept topped up as resources are destroyed. Why: a pool
  then starts no thread and holds no timer, and a program that wants eviction on a quiet pool calls
  `evictIdle` from a `Ticker`. Alternatives weighed: a reaper thread per pool (a thread that
  outlives every call and must be stopped by `close`); refilling to `minIdle` after each eviction
  (a `create` failing in the background has nobody to report to).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `api-pool`): **a pool's failure is
  `PoolError[E]`: `AcquireTimedOut`, `PoolClosed`, `CreateFailed(error: E)`.** It is an `Error`
  where `E` is, `CreateFailed` having `error` as its `cause`, and shows the same sentence wherever

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `pool-production`, for the PostgreSQL

  exhaustive `match` on `PoolError` elsewhere needs an arm.
