  kept. Each resource draws its part of `jitter`, from 0 up to `jitter`, once when it is made, and
  both its lifetime and its idle limit are lengthened by it; the draw comes from a SplitMix64
  generator of the pool's own under its lock, since `avin.random` builds on `avin.threads`. Adding
  rather than subtracting follows the PostgreSQL driver pgx (`MaxConnLifetimeJitter`), keeps
  every limit a true minimum, and needs no clamp when `jitter` exceeds a limit. Alternatives
  weighed: subtracting the jitter (a limit becomes a ceiling, which suits a server-side cutoff,
  but a jitter longer than the limit would need clamping); a jitter as a fraction of each limit;
  jitter on the lifetime only. **Review with the user**: subtracting is the other common choice.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (branch `pool-production`): **`counters()` answers a
  `PoolCounters` of running totals beside `stats()`, rather than widening `PoolStats`.** `acquires`,
  `waited`, `waitTime`, `timeouts`, `rejected`, `created` and `destroyed` are what a server exports as
  metrics (pgx's `Stat`, a pool's usual gauges); `PoolStats` stays the deterministic snapshot of what
  is held now, which tests and programs print, while `waitTime` varies run to run. `waitTime` runs
  from the call to the lending, so it includes making or checking a resource, as pgx's
  `AcquireDuration` does. Alternatives weighed: one wider `PoolStats` (its printed form would stop
  being stable); counting in each user's wrapper (`waited` and `timeouts` are only known under the
  lock).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `select-readable`): **a thread waits
  for a connection's bytes OR a channel's value with a `select` arm, `stream.readable() -> body`,
  not with a second waiting mechanism.** A connection belongs to one thread (its reference counts
  are not atomic, and OpenSSL is single-threaded per connection), so the thread that owns a
  WebSocket must do all of its reads and writes, and so must wait for "bytes arrived or another
  thread queued a frame". The arm fits the others' shape, an operation on its operand
  (`ch.receive()`, `ch.send(x)`), so it composes with channel arms, `after` and `else`, and the
  select's one-park, wake-once token covers it: where the stream is not readable when tried, its
  descriptor is registered with the runtime's poller for one report under the select's own waiter,
  and every ending withdraws it under the poller's lock, as channel links are withdrawn. The arm
  binds nothing and reads nothing (its body reads), since a read's size and form (`read(max)`,
  `readLine`) are the body's choice. Ready means a read would answer without waiting: buffered
  read-ahead, TLS plaintext already decrypted or a whole record arrived (TLS's `readable()` hands
  the engine the ciphertext already on the socket, so part of a record does not count, and keeps
  any failure it meets for the next read), the end, a reset or a closed connection. Its operand is
  the trait `avin.threads.Readiness` (`readable() -> bool`, `readinessDescriptor() -> int`), which
  `ByteStream` extends, so `avin.threads` needs nothing of `avin.net`, and a source of one's own,
  with `-1` for no descriptor, can be named too. The thread dump counts the arms as sockets ("in a
  select on 1 channel and 1 socket"). Alternatives weighed: an interruptible socket wait rung by a
  waker (smaller, but a second way to wait beside select, composing with neither `after` nor several
  channels); an arm that reads and binds the bytes, `conn.read(n) as bytes` (fixes the read's form
  in the arm, and a `readLine` could not use it); waking on socket readiness alone for TLS (a partial
  record would wake a select whose read then blocks). Review with the user: the spelling
  `readable()` and the name `Readiness`; whether the descriptor should stay a public method.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `ws-sender`): **a WebSocket's other
  threads send through `ws.sender()`, a sendable `WebSocketSender` that queues whole messages in a
  bounded outbox the owning thread writes while it receives.** The owner's `receive` waits in one
  `select` on the stream's `readable()`, the outbox, a sender's close request, the server's
  `stopped()` channel and the limit, so every frame (senders', its own, pongs, the close handshake)
  is written by the thread the connection belongs to, a message at a time, never interleaved.
  Alternatives weighed: a mutex around the socket shared by every writer (impossible: a TLS stream
  and a socket's handles belong to one thread); a writer thread per WebSocket (a second owner of the
  connection, the same impossibility); an unbounded outbox (a slow client would hold every message
  ever sent to it).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `ws-sender`): **the outbox is bounded
  in messages, `outboxSize = 64` on `webSocket` and `WebSocket.connect`, not in bytes; a send to a
  full one waits up to the WebSocket's write timeout and answers `Err(Broken(IoError(TimedOut, _,
  _)))`, the WebSocket left open.** A message bound is one bounded channel, and the owner's write to
  a client that does not read fails at the same write timeout, closing it, so a slow client holds at
  most 64 messages and its senders at most one write timeout each. Zero is a hand-over: each send
  waits for the owner to take it. Alternatives weighed: a byte bound (needs a second counter beside
  the channel, and one huge message would still have to be admitted); failing at once when full
  (a burst would lose messages a healthy client reads a moment later); closing the WebSocket when a
  send times out (the owner's write timeout already does, for a client that really stopped).
  Review with the user: whether a byte bound is wanted beside the message bound, and the default 64.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `ws-sender`): **`Ok` from a sender
  means queued while open; the close is a request, and the senders are refused from the start of
  any close.** A sender's `close(code, reason)` sets the shared state at once (every sender call
  after answers `Err(Closed(code, reason))`) and the owner carries it out while it receives, after
  writing what was queued before it. The owner's close refuses senders from the start of its
  handshake, and its end (close, peer close, failure, server stopping, cancellation) drops what is
  queued and wakes every sender waiting for room. A message queued in the instant the WebSocket
  ends may answer `Ok` and be dropped, as a write accepted by a socket that then breaks is.
  Alternatives weighed: an `Ok` only once written (every send would wait for the owner's next
  receive); closing from the sender's thread (it does not own the connection).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `ws-sender`): **a session that only
  answers what arrives loops in `ws.serve(onMessage) -> WebSocketError`**, which receives until the
  WebSocket closes and answers why, beside `receive()`, which a session may loop on itself; it is
  while the owner receives that its senders' messages are written, so a session must be in one or
  the other. Alternatives weighed: a background writer started by `sender()` (a second owner); no
  helper, documenting the `receive()` loop (the chat server's loop is written once in every app).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `ws-sender`): **data messages over
  65536 bytes are sent in fragments of 65536, written back to back**, by the owner's `send` and by
  senders alike, so a peer limiting frame sizes still takes large messages; a pong waits for the end
  of the message being written. A thread cancelled while it receives closes the connection with no
  close frame (a frame may have been half written) and ends the WebSocket with `1006`.
  `TcpServer.stopped()` is a channel closed by `stop`, which the owner's select watches in place of
  running each wait on a thread of its own through `idle`. Review with the user: the fragment size,
  and whether `stopped()` should be a receive-only view rather than a `Channel[unit]`.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `stdio-blocking`): **standard input
  and output wait safe for the collector.** Every read of standard input and every write to standard
  output or standard error, a flush and a trap's report included, marks its thread safe for the
  collector while it waits, the string being written kept in a frame of the runtime's own. A
  lightweight thread reading standard input from a stream with no position (a pipe, a socket, a
  terminal where the platform answers so) parks on the poller first; one reading a file or a device
  reads at once, since the poller does not report a file at its end as ready. Writes do not park: the
  output goes through the C library's buffer, shared with any C code the program calls, so a thread
  held up writing keeps its worker, counted as blocked, and the monitor runs another in its place.
  **The wait for standard input is not a cancellation point**, as it was not before: a cancelled
  thread goes on waiting for its line. *Why*: the smallest fix that keeps the behaviour the program
  sees; making it one would add a failure path to `readLine`, which answers no error. *Alternatives*:
  parking writes too (needs non-blocking standard output, which a pipe shared with the parent
  process cannot be given safely); a cancellable input wait that unwinds the thread as a sleep does.
  Review with the user: whether waiting for standard input should be a cancellation point.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `net-split-writable`): **a
  connection splits into a reader and a writer for two threads at once.** `ByteStream.split() ->
  (StreamReader, StreamWriter)`, for `TcpStream`, `UnixStream` and `TlsStream`; both halves are
  sendable traits, each half its own thread's, so a driver pipelines a batch of any size without
  stopping at windows for the send/receive buffer deadlock (found by the pg driver's batch item).
  Closing the writer half-closes (shutdown write; TLS sends its close notice first); closing the
  reader only stops reading; the connection closes once both halves are closed or unreachable.
  The split connection is used up (every operation answers an error naming the split; closing it
  does nothing); splitting it again, or splitting a closed connection, traps. **No `reunite`**: a
  protocol that wants one owner again keeps both halves on one thread, and a reunite would have to
  check that the two halves are of one connection and that neither has pending state. A TCP or Unix
  writer's `close` answers `Ok` where the peer has gone, as a connection's does; a TLS writer's answers
  whether the close notice went out, as `TlsStream.close` does. Each half holds its own handle on the
  socket (`avin.rt.socket_share`), so each is owner-checked on its own. The runtime's poller keeps,
  per descriptor, the waiter of each direction and registers the union of the two
  (`runtime/avin/rt/sockets.sysl`), so a reader parked for bytes and a writer parked for room wait
  on one descriptor at once; before this a second registration replaced the first under epoll. A TLS
  stream's halves share one session in a `@keeps_owners` object: the engine and the TCP writer are
  reached only holding a lock of their own, each handle taken from transit by the code holding the
  lock and handed back before it goes (a cancellation included, by `defer`), and nothing is held
  while waiting for the connection, so the reader decrypts while the writer waits for room. A reader
  that has ciphertext of its own to send sends it only where nobody else is sending (`tryAcquire`),
  and otherwise leaves it owed to the writer. Alternatives weighed: concurrent reads and writes on
  one connection value, with no halves (no owner check could then tell a misuse from a use);
  `dup`ing the descriptor for the writer (Sysl's `Socket` cannot adopt one, and the poller would
  still need two registrations under kqueue's filters); a TLS writer that waits for the reader on
  every record (a renegotiation alone needs that, and the writer does wait for it then).
  **Review with the user:** whether a reunite is wanted, and that a writer told by TLS to wait for
  the peer (a renegotiation) waits for its reader to read.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-15 (built on branch `net-split-writable`): **`writable()`
  is a select arm beside `readable()`, with a partial write `writeSome(bytes) -> Result[int,
  IoError]`.** `threads.Writability` (`writable()`, `writabilityDescriptor()`) beside `Readiness`;
  every `ByteStream` and every `StreamWriter` is one, and `select` reads `sink.writable()` into a
  `SelectWritable` arm, watched on the poller for room. `writeSome` is added because the arm needs
  it to be useful: `write` sends everything and so waits again after the arm said there was room.
  It waits for room for the first byte only where there is none, sends what fits, and answers at
  least one unless given nothing. Over TLS it hands TLS at most one record (16384 bytes of
  plaintext) and sends what of the record fits; the rest is kept and goes before anything else, and
  `writable()` sends it as room comes and answers `true` only once it has gone, so `writeSome` after
  `writable()` never waits; a read meanwhile leaves its own ciphertext queued behind that record
  rather than waiting for room. Alternatives weighed: no `writeSome`, the arm for `write` (waits
  again on a large write, as above); a TLS `writeSome` that sends its whole record (waits for room
  for a record after the arm said there was some); a `writable()` that ignores the kept record (a
  select that finds the socket writable and the arm not, round after round, spinning).
  **Review with the user:** the TLS record bound of `writeSome`, and the names `writeSome` and
  `writabilityDescriptor`.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (branch `read-secret`): **`io.readSecret(prompt)`,
  `readSecretBytes` and `readSecretOrLine` read a line from the controlling terminal with echo
  off.** fettle prompts for a sudo or ssh password, as does any tool asking for a passphrase, and
  nothing in the library read input with echo off. The calls open `/dev/tty` (so a piped standard
  input does not matter), write the prompt to it, turn off `ECHO` and `ECHONL` while keeping
  `ICANON`, and restore the exact `termios` found. Details settled: (1) **no terminal** is
  `Err(IoError(NoTerminal, "read", "the terminal"))`, a new `ErrorKind` case, since a program
  tells it apart from a failed read; `readSecretOrLine` is the opt-in fallback, writing the prompt
  to standard error and reading a line from standard input, as a tool run by a script with its
  password piped in needs. (2) **Signals**: `ISIG` stays on, and for the length of the read the C
  side (`runtime/avin/rt/__posix__/secret_tty.c`) catches interrupt, hangup, terminate and quit: its
  handler restores the terminal, gives the signal its previous action back and sends it again, so
  the program dies or handles the signal with echo on; a program that survives sees the read fail
  as `Other("interrupted")`. A terminal stop (Ctrl-Z) is caught too: the handler restores the
  terminal, stops the program with the default action, and on continue hides the terminal again
  and the read writes its prompt again and goes on (as `sudo` and `getpass` do); what was typed before
  the Ctrl-Z is discarded by the terminal. SIGTTIN and SIGTTOU are not caught: they stop a program before the terminal has been
  changed. (3) **Concurrency**: the read holds
  `input_readers`, the lock of every standard input reader, so a secret and a `readLine` never
  read the terminal at once; a lightweight thread waiting for the line is not cancellable, as one
  waiting for standard input is, so a cancel takes effect once the line has been read and the
  terminal is back. (4) **Bytes**: `readSecretBytes` returns an `Array[byte]` the caller can
  overwrite; `readSecret` is a string, which has no way to be cleared, and the runtime clears its
  own gathering buffers. (5) A trailing `\n` and a `\r` before it are dropped; the end of input
  with bytes typed ends the line, with none it is `Other("end of input")`. Alternatives weighed:
  turning `ISIG` off as `getpass` does (Ctrl-C then arrives as a byte only once the line ends,
  so it would not interrupt a prompt); reading standard input when there is no terminal by default
  (a secret would then show on the screen, and a program that means to read one must ask by
  name); a cancellable wait (the existing standard input lock holds the thread's cancellation off,
  and a read cut short would leave typed bytes half taken); a single `readSecret` with a
  fallback flag. Tests drive real programs over a pseudo-terminal (`tests/pty/pty_drive.c`,
  `secret_tests.sysl`). **Review with the user:** the name `readSecret` (against `readPassword`
  or `promptSecret`), and the no-terminal behaviour: an error by default with `readSecretOrLine`
  as the explicit fallback, rather than falling back to standard input on its own.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (branch `stdio-bytes`): **`io.stdin()` is standard
  input as a `Reader` of bytes, and `io.stdout()` and `io.stderr()` are standard output and error
  as `ByteWriter`s**, answering the `Sendable` objects `StandardInputBytes`, `StandardOutputBytes`
  and `StandardErrorBytes`. Source: the avin-lang/lsp package could not serve LSP over stdio, whose
  `Content-Length` counts bytes, since `avin.io` read standard input only as text decoded with
  U+FFFD and had no byte writer for standard output; the workaround would have bound Sysl's
  `FdReader` directly, as the tui package does. Details settled: (1) **Mixing**: byte reads take
  from the one buffer `readLine`, `lines()`, `readAll` and `Source.stdin()` share
  (`runtime/avin/rt/input.sysl`), so a header read as a line and a body read as bytes go on from
  each other with no byte lost or read twice; a read answers what the buffer holds, else one read
  of the input. (2) **Serialization**: byte reads hold `input_readers`, the lock of every standard
  input reader and of `readSecret`. (3) **Parking**: a lightweight thread waits on the poller, as a
  line read does. (4) **End and failure**: the end is an empty array, every time it is asked; a
  read that fails is `Err(Other(<platform sentence>))` for bytes, while the text readers keep seeing
  the end. (5) **Output**: a byte write is unbuffered and goes out whole before it returns, behind
  what `print` buffered: it holds standard output's stdio lock while flushing that buffer and
  writing to the descriptor, and `println` writes its whole line through the same stream, so a
  printed line is never split by a byte write (the println-atomic entry of 2026-11-15 still holds);
  a write to standard error flushes standard output first, as `eprint` does. (6) **A reader that
  has gone**: SIGPIPE is held off for the length of a byte write (on macOS by the descriptor's own
  mark, the 2026-11-20 entry below; elsewhere blocked on the writing thread, the one the write
  raised taken back), so the write answers `ConnectionReset` (`EPIPE`, the kind a
  connection's write answers) and the program goes on; `print` keeps its quiet death, which a
  filter in a pipeline wants. (7) **Closed descriptors**: a bug met on the way, a program started
  with standard input closed read the runtime's own pipe, which had taken descriptor 0; the runtime
  now opens `/dev/null` on each of 0, 1 and 2 that is missing before it opens anything. Alternatives
  weighed: an error for mixing text and byte reads (two buffers or a mode switch, and a header and
  body protocol could not be written at all); a buffered `stdout()` with `flush` (a byte write
  could then be overtaken by, or split, a `println`, and an LSP message must leave whole); ignoring
  SIGPIPE for the whole program (every `print` to a closed pipe would then have to fail somewhere,
  where today it ends the program quietly); public objects alone with no functions (a module-level
  function reads as `io.readLine()` does). Tests: `stdio_tests.sysl`, driving
  `tests/stdio/stdio_bytes.avin` through `sh` and `tests/pty/stdio_tty.avin` over a
  pseudo-terminal, at -O0 and -O2. **Review with the user:** the names `stdin()`, `stdout()`,
  `stderr()` and the object names `StandardInputBytes`, `StandardOutputBytes`,
  `StandardErrorBytes` (beside the text writers `StandardOutput` and `StandardError`).
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-20 (branch `stdio-sigpipe`): **on macOS a byte write
    to standard output or error marks the descriptor never to raise SIGPIPE (`F_SETNOSIGPIPE`) for
    the length of the write only**, and puts back the mark it found. WHY: macOS raises the SIGPIPE
    of a write to a gone reader on the whole process, where any thread not blocking it takes it, so
    blocking it on the writing thread (item (6) above) failed whenever the program had another
    thread: four threads writing to `prog | head -c 10`, or one writer beside busy threads, ended
    with status 141 every time at -O0 and -O2 before the change. The mark belongs to the open pipe
    or socket, which the shell and the program's children share, so it is held under the stdio
    locks of both standard streams and taken off before the write returns: `print`, `eprint` and a
    child writing to the same output keep their SIGPIPE, and nothing is left changed on the shell's
    pipe after the program ends. On Linux the signal goes to the writing thread, so the thread mask
    is kept there unchanged. ALTERNATIVES: marking descriptors 1 and 2 once at startup (every
    `print` to a gone reader would then fail silently and a printing loop would never end, every
    child and every later process on the shell's pipe would inherit the mark); ignoring SIGPIPE for
    the whole program (the same `print` problem, and an ignored signal survives `exec` into every
    child). Tests: `stdio_tests.sysl` § several writing threads, a writer beside busy threads,
    threads writing to standard error, `print` without a newline after a failed byte write, and a
    child (`yes`) started after one, at -O0 and -O2.

- **Linux as a target, and machines in packages** (branch `linux-plan`, 2026-11-19; the user,
  2026-11-19: Avin is "for anyone who would enjoy using it"). The plan is
  [Linux](/compiler/linux/); the package surface is [machines](/spec/packages/#machines).
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19: **Avin's targets are `aarch64-macos`,
    `x86_64-linux` and `aarch64-linux`**, glibc on Linux, named as Sysl's target registry names
    them. WHY: they are Sysl's release platforms, so the toolchain Avin drives at every build
    exists on each; servers and CI are overwhelmingly x86_64 Linux, and aarch64 Linux is what a
    Mac's containers run natively. ALTERNATIVES: x86_64 Linux alone (leaves out Arm servers and
    makes every local Linux test an emulated one); musl (static executables, but Sysl's registry
    and its library are glibc's); Intel macOS and Windows (Sysl ships neither).
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19: **Avin is built natively on each target, not
    cross-compiled from the Mac.** WHY: an installed Avin runs `sysl build-c` and clang at every
    user's build, so Linux needs Sysl and clang on Linux whatever the release does, and a native
    build is the configuration users run; cross-building would add a sysroot to manage for no
    user. Local Linux work runs in a colima VM (aarch64, native speed on Apple silicon) through
    marshal; CI runs GitHub's x86_64 and arm64 Ubuntu runners. ALTERNATIVES: cross-compiling from
    the Mac with a glibc sysroot (Sysl cannot yet: the probe of `sysl build --target x86_64-linux`
    fails building its standard module, `stdio.h` not found, and Sysl has no way to name a sysroot);
    both (cross kept for `avin build --target`, a later item once Sysl has sysroots).
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19: **a Linux release ships a tarball per target**
    (`avin-<v>-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`, `avin-<v>-linux-arm64.tar.gz`, the same prefix layout as the
    macOS one) **and an install script** that installs Avin and the Sysl it needs into a prefix
    and names the distribution's packages for clang, lld, llvm-ar and pkg-config; the Homebrew
    formula gains `on_linux` once Sysl's formula has it. No `.deb`. WHY: a tarball is what every
    other route is built from, and an install script reaches every distribution with no
    repository to host or sign. ALTERNATIVES: Linuxbrew only (needs Sysl's formula on Linux first,
    and many servers have no brew); a `.deb` and an apt repository (hosting and signing, one
    distribution family); a static single binary (Avin needs Sysl and clang beside it anyway).
    **Review with the user:** whether a `.deb` is wanted later.
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19: **machine conditions in the manifest are Sysl's
    condition language** (symbols, `!`, `&&`, `||`, parentheses), over the closed set `macos`,
    `linux`, `posix`, `aarch64`, `x86_64`, as `if` on an entry of `dependencies`,
    `sysl-dependencies` and `c-libraries` and on a feature (where it says only where the feature
    exists), checked symbol by symbol when the manifest is read; `package.targets` lists the
    targets a package supports (all by default); `install` may be a block of sentences by
    condition; `link-flags` passes flags such as `-framework Security` as written. `avin tidy` and
    `avin vendor` answer for every target. WHY: one condition language across Avin's manifest,
    Sysl's manifests and the Sysl dependencies Avin hands to Sysl; checking every symbol at read
    keeps a misspelling from silently dropping a dependency. ALTERNATIVES: per-target blocks
    (`targets.x86_64-linux { dependencies { … } }`, which repeat a dependency per target and
    cannot say "every Linux"); a target name as the condition (`if = "x86_64-linux"`, which cannot
    say "every Linux" either); Sysl's `choices` and per-target linker keys (machine and image
    configuration Avin's hosted programs do not have).
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19: **in source, the file is the unit a machine
    selects**: `name.<symbol>.avin` is read only where the symbol holds, a module exists on a
    machine where any of its files is read, an import of a module that is not everywhere is allowed
    only from a file that is read no more widely, and `avin check` type-checks once per target
    where anything differs. Values that differ by machine are written over `avin.target.os` and
    `avin.target.arch`, compile-time constants whose untaken branches fold away, both branches
    checked on every machine. WHY: it keeps the rule features follow (a whole unit is in or out,
    nothing in a file changes with the build), so every file means one thing; a module keeps one
    name and one surface on every machine, and the per-target check proves the surface is there.
    ALTERNATIVES: Sysl's `#if` lines (a file reads differently per machine and the untaken lines
    are never checked); a constant alone (cannot hold a call only one system declares, since both
    branches are checked); whole modules per machine in the manifest (a `machines { linux { modules
    = […] } }` block, which forces shared code to import a different module per machine);
    `name_linux.avin` with an underscore (collides with ordinary file names that end in a system's
    name). **Review with the user:** the surface syntax: the `.linux.avin` infix,
    `package.targets`, the `if` key, the `install` block and `avin.target`.
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (closing two Open items): **a feature has no
    compile-time constant**, the module staying the only unit a feature gates. WHY: a feature's
    modules and optional dependencies are absent with it off, so a branch on `feature("x")` could
    not type-check against them; a machine constant works only because every machine's standard
    library is whole. ALTERNATIVES: a `feature("x")` constant folded away (fails to check, as
    above); line gates (the conditional compilation the features design refused). **A module is
    listed by one feature only**; a part two features share becomes a feature both `enables`.
    WHY: every gate stays one feature, so the import check stays one question. ALTERNATIVES: a
    module on while any of its features is on (the import check would have to reason about
    disjunctions, and a module's presence would depend on combinations).
  - Found while surveying, not fixed here (no runtime run is allowed on this branch): the DNS
    lookup's pipe sets descriptor flag `2` (`runtime/avin/rt/lookup.sysl`, `CloseOnExecFlag`), but
    `FD_CLOEXEC` is `1` on macOS and on Linux, so the pipe is inherited by a child started during a
    lookup. macOS hides it, starting children with every other descriptor closed; Linux does not.
    It is the first item of the [plan](/compiler/linux/).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (the user approved moving extractors onto a trait the
  same day; branch `extractor-trait`): **an extractor is a value whose type implements one of three
  core traits**, `Extractor[-A, +B]` (`unapply(value: A) -> Option[B]`), `BoolExtractor[-A]`
  (`unapply(value: A) -> bool`) and `SeqExtractor[-A, +S]` (`unapplySeq(value: A) -> Option[S]`),
  in `library/avin/extractor.avin`; the pattern checker finds the conformance (`extractor_instances`
  in `check.sysl`) and calls the trait's method, a class's or data type's own implementation
  directly, so a method merely named `unapply` no longer makes an extractor. The pattern syntax, the
  three result shapes, coverage (an extractor never counts) and refinement (an extractor learns no
  equalities) are unchanged, and the methods keep the names `unapply` and `unapplySeq`. A type
  implements each trait at one type argument (the rule for every trait with instance members); the
  trait whose `A` takes the matched value serves, an `unapply` trait before `SeqExtractor`. A
  type's name is no extractor. A value implementing none is reported with the trait to implement,
  worked out from the type's own `unapply` or `unapplySeq` where it has one, or with the three
  traits and their methods. WHY: the user's rule that Avin is sound and nominal, which the soundness
  audit found broken here by a lookup by name; as ordinary traits, extractors also become
  first-class: held in a value of the trait's type, passed as a parameter, bounded on a type
  parameter, implemented by a data type through an impl, inherited by a subclass, with the
  variance a function's argument and result have. The `S` of `SeqExtractor` is left open rather
  than bounded by `Seq`, so a `List` stays a `List` for its `rest*` and list patterns; the pattern
  asks for a sequence where it is used. ALTERNATIVES: a marker trait with no members, the method
  still found by name inside it (half nominal; a value of the trait's type could not be matched);
  one trait with the result shape as a type parameter (the three shapes are different methods);
  `unapply` keeping its role by name with a modifier (not a trait, so no extractor values).
  **Review with the user:** two things the structural rule allowed are gone: an extractor object
  with a generic method, `object Pair` with `unapply[A](xs: List[A])`, which no trait instance can
  name, is now a generic class used through a value (`val pair = Pair[A]()`, `pair(a, b)`); and
  one object with `unapply`s overloaded on several input types now picks one input type per trait.
  Each implementation is also written `override`, as every trait member's is.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (built on branch `builder-trait`; the move onto a trait
  approved by the user 2026-11-19): **a collection literal finds its builder through the core trait
  `Buildable[A]`, never by a method's name** ([literals](/spec/collections/#literals)). The trait has
  one member, `static newBuilder() -> Builder[A, Self]`; `A` is the element a literal gives the
  builder, a map's `(K, V)` pair. A literal where a type `C` is expected is built by `C.newBuilder()`
  where an impl of `Buildable` targets `C` itself, or where `C` is a type parameter bounded by it
  (`make[C: Buildable[int]]() -> C = [1, 2, 3]`); otherwise it is the default `Vector`, `Set` or
  `Map`, built through their own conformances. A companion object's `newBuilder` builds no literal.
  Every library collection implements it, its impl calling the companion's `newBuilder`, which stays
  the public way to get a builder (`Vector.newBuilder[int]()`); a repeated parameter's vector is
  built through `Vector`'s conformance too. An expected collection (an `Iterable`, or a type whose
  companion has a `newBuilder`) that is neither `Buildable` nor an instance of the default is
  reported by the trait it lacks: "a sequence literal cannot build `Stack[int]`, which does not
  implement `Buildable`…". WHY: the user's goal is a sound, nominally typed language, and a literal
  that called whatever its expected type's companion named `newBuilder` was the last structural
  lookup the soundness audit left; a trait is a stated promise, checked where it is made. One trait
  for sequences, sets and maps, parameterized by the element rather than by a type constructor,
  serves every collection the library has: `BitSet` (a `Buildable[int]` with no parameter of its
  own), `TreeSet` (an `Ord` bound on its impl), maps (pairs), traits (`Set`, `SortedMap`, building
  their default kinds), and any program's collection, with or without a companion, from any module,
  as `FromInteger` does for integer literals. **The conformance is the type's own**: a `TreeSet`
  expected is built by `TreeSet`'s impl, never by `SortedSet`'s or `Set`'s, since those would make
  a different collection. ALTERNATIVES: a constructor trait on the companion, `trait
  IterableFactory[C[_]]` with `newBuilder[A]()` (cannot express `BitSet`, which takes no
  parameter, nor `TreeSet`'s `Ord` and `HashSet`'s `Eq & Hash` element bounds, and needs a second
  trait for maps); two traits, one for sequences and sets and one for maps (the element type already
  tells a pair from an element, so the second adds nothing); removing the companions' `newBuilder`
  and calling the static as `Vector[int].newBuilder()` (breaks every call site in every avin-lang
  repo for no gain in soundness). A trait type's own conformance builds where the trait type is
  expected (`SortedSet`, `Set`, `Map`, `SeqMap`, so `{}` where a `Map` is expected is the empty map
  through `Map`'s own impl), and an impl for one instance, `impl Buildable[int] for Count[int]`,
  builds that instance only; `Count[string]` expected is the error naming the trait. **The companion
  `apply` stays an ordinary method** (`Deque(1, 2, 3)`): its repeated parameter's `Vector` is already
  built through `Vector`'s conformance, so it meets the trait where a literal does, and each
  collection keeps the cheapest way from that vector to itself. ALTERNATIVES for `apply`: rewriting
  every companion `apply` over its own `newBuilder` (no gain in soundness, and slower where `apply`
  converts the vector directly, as `Array`'s `toArray` does); a `static apply(xs: A*) -> Self` in
  `Buildable` with a default body (makes `C(1, 2)` callable on a bound `C: Buildable[int]`, but adds
  a second member every program's impl inherits, and `C.newBuilder()` already serves that).
  **Review with the user**: the name `Buildable`, and whether the companions' `newBuilder` should
  eventually be the static member alone.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (branch `train-ay`, reconciling `builder-trait` with
  the comparisons of ranges and literals that predate it): **a type only suggested to a collection
  literal, by another operand of `==`, `!=` or an ordering, leaves the literal its default where no
  literal builds that type**, so `(1 .. 3) == [1, 2, 3]` is
  a `Range` compared with a `Vector` by their elements, as before `Buildable`; a type demanded of
  the literal (a declaration, a parameter, a result, an ascription) still reports the trait it
  lacks, `val r: Range = [1, 2]`. WHY: the suggestion exists so a literal compares like with like
  where it can (`xs == [1, 2]` with `xs` a `List`); where it cannot, a literal of the default
  compares the same by `Seq` equality, and an error there would refuse a comparison that has an
  obvious meaning. ALTERNATIVES: refusing the comparison and asking for `.toVector` (breaks
  established programs for no soundness gain); making `Range` `Buildable` (a literal cannot promise
  a range's even step, so its builder would have to fail at run time).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (branch `train-ay`, reconciling `bytes-sendable`'s
  `object Isolated` with constructors used as values): **a class's companion object that declares no
  `apply` leaves the name the class's constructor where a function is expected**, as in call
  position, so `val mi: (Vector[string]) -> Isolated[Vector[string]] = Isolated` and
  `[1, 2].map(Box)` make values; elsewhere the name is the object. WHY: adding a companion with
  unrelated members (`Isolated.move`) must not take away the constructor value its class had.
  ALTERNATIVES: the object always (breaks every such value when a companion is added); an error
  asking to choose (nothing is ambiguous where the object is not a function).

- **`avin repl`, an interactive session** (branch `repl`, 2026-11-19; approved by the user the same
  day). The surface is in [getting started](/getting-started/#the-interactive-session).
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19: **a session is one growing program, built and run
    whole after each input; earlier inputs run again, their output passed over.** Imports go to the
    program's top, type declarations below them, everything else into `main`; the program writes a
    mark before the newest input and one after it, and only what lies between is shown. WHY: Avin
    compiles a closed world — one LLVM module with the library, monomorphized instances, devirtualized
    calls and per-program type descriptors — so loading each input as a shared object into one live
    process (keeping the heap, globals and threads) needs separate compilation across units:
    instances shared or duplicated between units, type identity across them, the collector's roots
    registered per loaded unit, and the runtime moved into the host. That is a compiler architecture,
    not an item. Replaying costs an input's side effects repeating unseen, values computed afresh
    (random, time) differing from the ones shown, and run time growing with the session; each input
    still builds in about a second at `-O0` through the instance cache. ALTERNATIVES: `dlopen` per
    input into a live process (the right end state, above); an interpreter over the checked program
    (a second semantics to keep equal to the compiled one); replaying with the earlier inputs'
    effects suppressed (not possible for effects outside the process). **Review with the user:**
    whether the live-process design is wanted next, and how soon.
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19: **each code input is a block nested in the one
    before it** (`if true` around the rest), so `val x` entered again hides the earlier `x` from the
    later inputs, as a block's local does, and the earlier inputs keep the `x` they saw; a local
    function entered again does the same. WHY: Avin forbids a second `val` of one name in one block;
    nesting gives the hiding every interactive language has without renaming anything.
    ALTERNATIVES: renaming earlier bindings (rewrites what the user typed, and diagnostics show other
    names).
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (branch `repl-2`; replaces "functions are local
    functions of `main`" and "a type declared again replaces the earlier declaration"): **each
    declaration of types, and each function or `val` that uses no local of `main`, is a module of the
    session's own** (`avinrepl.c3`), which imports, by name, the newest of each name the inputs
    before it gave, and every earlier module whole (so their extensions are seen). Such a function or
    `val` is *hoisted*: a class, trait or function entered after it calls or reads it. A hoisted
    function is also written into `main` where it was entered, and a hoisted `val` read there under
    its name (`val base = avinReplC2.base`), so code in `main` sees every name in the order entered,
    exactly as before. A name entered again hides the earlier one from every later input, module or
    code, and a module entered before keeps the one it imported: a class calling `twice` keeps the
    `twice` it was declared after. "Uses no local" is the checker's answer, not a guess: the input is
    first checked and run as code of `main`, and hoisted when none of its references resolve to a
    local of `main` other than a hoisted input's. A hoisted input is written as a module only once a
    declaration of types comes after it (nothing else can reach it there), so a session of code
    alone checks and builds no extra files; one that does not check as a module when a declaration
    first needs it stays code of `main`, and the declaration is checked again without it. A function
    or `val` that uses a local stays in `main`, and a `var`, a `lazy val`, a
    destructuring `val` and an input of several statements stay there too, out of the modules'
    reach; a module never imports a name whose newest declaration is such a local. `main` imports the
    newest of each type's name, so code there sees a type declared again in place of the old one,
    and the new declaration is refused where earlier code of `main` no longer checks against it. An
    impl of a type or trait the session declared joins that declaration's module, where a
    conformance has to be and a plain impl's methods are the type's own; any other impl is an
    extension in a module of its own. A session import binding a name a module gives is left out of
    the later modules, the module's name being the nearer. A hoisted `val` is computed before `main`
    when the session runs again, which is not seen: an earlier input's output is passed over.
    WHY: a declaration can only reach what is declared at the top level of some module, and modules
    are how Avin scopes names, so one module per input gives declarations the same hiding `main`
    has, with nothing renamed and every diagnostic in the user's own names; and each module's text is
    fixed once entered, so its instances stay in the build cache. ALTERNATIVES: one top-level module
    for every declaration (a function or `val` entered again would replace the earlier one under the
    inputs that used it, and a value computed from it would change when the session runs again);
    hoisting by renaming (`twice$2`; diagnostics and types show the other names); hoisting by a
    syntactic test of the free names (a parameter named like a local would keep the function local).
    **Review with the user:** that code of `main` sees a type declared again where modules keep the
    old one (Avin has no local types to hide it with), and whether a `var` should be reachable from
    declarations too (a module-level `var` changes what threads may read).
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19: **an expression's value is kept as `resN` and shown
    as `res0: int = 42`, by its type's `Debug` through `Any`** (a string quoted, a type with no
    `Debug` by its name, a function as `<function>`); a `val` or `var` shows its own name, a local
    function its header, a type declaration its header; an expression of type `unit` shows nothing
    and takes no number. The type is the checker's, as hover shows it. ALTERNATIVES: `Display`
    (a string unquoted reads like output); `it` for the last value only.
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19: **an input ends** at the end of its line unless a
    bracket is open, the line ends with an operator, `=` or a comma, or the input opened a block —
    a type's declaration, a line the parser finds unfinished at its end (`if x > 0`, `f(n: int) ->
    int`), or a local function's header with parameters (`log(m: string)`, which alone reads as a
    call) — which an empty line ends. `greet()` alone is a call; a function of no parameters opens
    its block with a result type or `=`. ALTERNATIVES: a continuation character; always waiting for
    an empty line after an indented line (one more Enter for every one-line input).
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (branch `repl-2`, replacing `sysl.term.edit`,
    which edits one line and completes nothing): **at a terminal an input is edited whole by the
    session's own editor** (`repl_editor.sysl`, over `sysl.term.keys`): Enter enters an input the
    completeness rule above finds complete, wherever the cursor is, and otherwise breaks the line at
    the cursor and goes on under a `    | ` prompt, indented as the line above and two more after a
    line opening a block (`if`, `else`, a header, an open bracket, a trailing operator; a trailing
    comma keeps the indentation); Backspace over an indentation takes back two columns; the arrows
    move through the input's lines and, past its first or last, through the inputs entered before
    (500, whole); Ctrl-A/E/B/F/P/N/K/U as usual, Ctrl-C drops the input, Ctrl-D on an empty one ends
    the session. Lines wider than the terminal are drawn over as many rows as they take (its width is
    asked at each drawing). Raw mode only while an input is read, so a running input gets Ctrl-C;
    **read from a pipe there are no prompts**, and lines are taken one at a time as before, so a
    scripted session's output is what its inputs write. An input's standard output and error reach
    the session as one stream, in the order written. No new C dependency. ALTERNATIVES: linenoise
    (a C dependency); a line at a time with a continuation prompt (an earlier line cannot be
    changed); entering on an empty line always (one more Enter for every one-line input).
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (branch `repl-2`): **Tab completes from the
    language server's completion** (`completion.sysl`): the input is placed in the session's
    program as it would be entered (an import among the imports, a declaration of types as a module
    of its own, other code in `main`), the word at the cursor replaced by the stand-in, and what the
    check finds there is offered: names in scope (locals of `main`, hoisted inputs, types, imports,
    the core library, and the keywords an expression may begin with), a receiver's members after a
    `.`, modules after `import`. The names are ordered nearest scope first, then by name; Tab writes
    what all of them begin with, and when that adds nothing and there are several, lists them under
    the input. Tab with only spaces before the cursor indents. The session's own names
    (`avinReplShow`, the module aliases) are never offered. ALTERNATIVES: names collected from the
    session's text (no members, no types of expressions); a menu to choose from (a larger editor).
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19: **in a package, or a directory holding a program,
    the session's program is that program with its root module replaced by the session**, so its
    modules import as they do from `main`, and its dependencies, Sysl packages and C libraries come
    with it. `:load <file>` enters a file's imports and top-level declarations one at a time as if
    typed; its `main` becomes a local function to call. ALTERNATIVES: keeping the root module
    (its `main` collides with the session's); `:load` running the file's `main` (it can be called).

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (proposed 2026-11-13 on branch `given-design`, the
  design approved by the user 2026-11-13 and its build approved 2026-11-19; built from branch
  `given-1` on): **contextual parameters are for context values, never for
  conformances** ([contextual parameters](/spec/contextual-parameters/)). A `using` parameter is
  filled from a `given` in scope; a bound is met only by the type's `impl`, a given never overrides
  or adds to one, a contextual parameter's type names no type parameter, and a given has none. Why:
  Avin already resolves trait instances coherently through `impl` and bounds, so letting a given
  fill a bound would be a second way to supply an instance, and an incoherent one: a `TreeSet`
  built under one ordering and searched under another. Under the principle the user set the same
  day (*"the ultimate SOUND, NOMINALLY typed, compiled, garbage-collected high-level language"*),
  coherence is not negotiable, so givens carry what conformances cannot: a transaction, a logger,
  a request, a clock. A non-natural order stays an argument of its call (`sortWith`, `sortBy` with
  `Reverse`). Alternatives weighed: a `using` of a trait type filled by a given, falling back to the
  impl (two ways to do one thing, and incoherent across values built under different scopes);
  givens for bounds only with priorities (the search and ambiguity rules that cost compile time and
  predictability); no contextual parameters at all (every layer threads a logger by hand).
  **Review with the user.** This is the central choice.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (proposed 2026-11-13 on branch `given-design`; built
  on branch `given-1`): **every given is named; no anonymous givens.**
  `given tx = db.begin()`, `given log: Logger = …`. Why: one way to declare one; the name is what a
  call passes explicitly (`tx = …`), what a diagnostic names and what another file imports.
  Alternatives weighed: anonymous `given RequestContext(id)` (a second form for the same thing, and
  an import with nothing to name); `given existingName` to make a value a given (a second way to
  make a lambda's parameter one, beside `using`). Review with the user: anonymous givens are the
  likeliest to be missed.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (proposed 2026-11-13 on branch `given-design`; built
  on branch `given-1`): **`using` is a trailing section of the one parameter
  list**, `f(a: A, using tx: Tx, log: Logger)`, passed explicitly only by name. Why: Avin has one
  parameter list per function and named arguments already; positional passing would let an
  argument meant for an ordinary parameter land on a contextual one. Alternatives weighed: a second
  parameter list `f(a)(using tx)` (Avin has no curried lists); `using` on each parameter (repetition);
  positional explicit passing (ambiguous next to defaults).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (proposed 2026-11-13 on branch `given-design`; to be
  built at step 3 of the [plan](/compiler/roadmap/#contextual-parameters-build-plan)): **resolution is lexical, nearest level wins, two fits
  at one level are an error**: blocks, then enclosing functions' and lambdas' `using` parameters,
  the class constructor's or actor's, the object's givens, then the module's own givens with the
  file's imported ones; fit is nominal conformance; then the parameter's default. Why: one
  deterministic answer per call, decided where it is written and shown by the source; no ranking by
  specificity, so no rule a reader must simulate. Alternatives weighed: exact-type matching only (a
  given `FileLogger` could not fill a `Logger`); most-specific ranking across levels (search, and
  surprising winners); one flat scope (a block could not narrow a module's given).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (proposed 2026-11-13 on branch `given-design`; to be
  built at step 4 of the plan): **a given is seen in another file only when imported
  by name** (directly or through an export); importing the module whole does not bring its givens.
  Why: a given changes what a call receives with nothing written at the call, so the file says
  which; a library adding a given then cannot change an existing call elsewhere. Alternatives
  weighed: givens seen through any import of their module, as extensions are (silent changes of
  meaning); a `.given` wildcard import (Avin has no wildcard import). Review with the user.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (proposed 2026-11-13 on branch `given-design`; built
  on branch `given-1`): **a given's type is a nominal type of the program**
  (a class, an object's type, a trait used as a type, a `data` type, closed type arguments); built-in
  types, tuples, function types and unions are refused, and a given is a `val`. Why: nominal typing
  — a value fills a parameter because its type declares what it is, not because a common shape such
  as `int` fits; and a `var` given would share a box across closures and threads.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (proposed 2026-11-13 on branch `given-design`; built
  on branch `given-1`): **givens are declared in blocks, at a module's top
  level and in object bodies; classes and actors take context as `using` parameters of their
  constructors** (private fields, givens in their bodies). No `given` in class, trait or `data`
  bodies, and none of `data` variants, `main`, tests, hooks or bindings take a `using` section. Why:
  one place per kind of declaration; a class's context comes from whoever makes it.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (proposed 2026-11-13 on branch `given-design`; to be
  built at step 5 of the plan): **lambdas and function values.** A lambda resolves
  where it is written and captures the givens it uses; its parameters after `using` are givens in
  its body but positional in its type; function types have no `using` section; a function taken as a
  value has its section filled where it is taken. Why: a function value is called with positional
  arguments only (as for names and defaults), and lexical capture keeps one rule for every closure.
  Alternatives weighed: contextual function types (`(using Tx) -> R`, a new kind of type); a
  `given tx` statement in the lambda's body (a second way). Review with the user: contextual
  function types are what would make `db.transaction { insert(row) }` need no parameter.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (proposed 2026-11-13 on branch `given-design`; to be
  built at step 5 of the plan): **a given does not cross `spawn` by itself**; a
  closure that uses one captures it and is checked as any capture (sendability, no `var`). Why: a
  given is a lexical value, not thread-local state, so the sharing rules see it. Alternatives
  weighed: an inherited per-thread context (dynamic scoping, invisible in the source).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (proposed 2026-11-13 on branch `given-design`; the
  section built on branch `given-1`, its filling at step 3 of the plan): **contextual parameters may have defaults**, used
  where no given fits, and every default of the function sees the contextual parameters, which are
  filled first. The section takes no part in choosing an overload. Why: a default is the natural
  fallback (`using clock: Clock = SystemClock`), and resolving after the overload is chosen keeps
  the cost of a call linear and its errors at the chosen function. No standard-library API adopts
  contextual parameters in this design; adopting one (an `Executor` for `Future(body)`) is its own
  item, since `ex.future(body)` already exists and the two would be two ways.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (branch `given-1`): **an opaque type may be a given's
  and a contextual parameter's type**, beside classes, objects, traits used as types and `data`
  types. Why: the refusal of built-in types exists because a given `int` would be given wherever
  any `int` is asked for; an opaque type is a nominal type of its own (`opaque type UserId =
  long`), which only what asks for a `UserId` receives, so it has none of that problem, and "avin is
  for everyone" favours the wider rule. Alternatives weighed: refusing it as the design's list did
  (a wrapper `data` type would be needed for a value an opaque type already names). Review with
  the user.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (branch `given-1`): **where `given` and `using`
  begin their forms.** `given` begins a given where a name and its `:` or `=` follow it; before
  `val`, `var` or a capitalized name it is read as a given and reported (a `val` already; never a
  `var`; every given named); everywhere else it is a name. `using` begins a section where a name
  (or a class parameter's modifier) follows it in a parameter list, also in a parenthesized lambda
  and as `using tx ->`, alone or as a call's trailing lambda. Why: the smallest test that keeps
  every existing use (`args.given(…)`, `given = 3`, `given(x)`, a parameter `using: Mode`) meaning
  what it did; the capitalized-name case turns the likeliest mistake, an unnamed given, into its
  own message rather than a parse error. Alternatives weighed: reserving both words (breaks
  existing programs); reading `given` before any name as a declaration (an infix call `given max
  b` on a value named `given` would change meaning).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (branch `given-1`): **a contextual parameter has a
  name, is neither by-name nor repeated, and a class's is written without `val`, `var` or
  `private`; a repeated parameter may come just before the section.** Why: it is passed explicitly
  only by name; a given is one value already made, so by-name evaluation and repetition mean
  nothing for it; a class's contextual parameter is a private field and a given by definition.
  The section comes last, so a repeated parameter is last of the others (`all(xs: int*, using tx:
  Tx)`). A data variant takes no section, reported where it is parsed.
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (branch `given-3`): **a local function's or a lambda's
  contextual parameters are a level of the scope walk between its body and the block it is written
  in**, so they beat the givens of the blocks around it and lose to the givens of its own body's
  blocks. Why: the chapter listed "the enclosing blocks" before "the contextual parameters of each
  enclosing function or lambda", which read literally would let a block outside a local function hide
  the function's own `using` parameter, the value its caller chose for it; resolving by lexical
  nearness is the rule every other name follows, and it is the reading of "nearer level wins" a
  reader expects. Alternatives weighed: every block first, then every function's parameters
  innermost out (the literal list, where `helper(using tx: Tx) = tag()` written in a block with
  `given t = Tx(…)` would ignore its own `tx`).
- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (branch `given-3`): **the section's defaults are
  computed before the other omitted defaults, and a contextual parameter's default sees the
  section's parameters before it, not the ordinary ones**; an ordinary default sees the parameters
  before it and the whole section. Why: the chapter has ordinary defaults see the section, so the
  section must be complete first; a section default that also saw ordinary parameters could depend
  on an ordinary default that depends on it, a cycle with no order to compute it in. Alternatives
  weighed: a section default seeing every parameter before it in the list (needs an order that
  interleaves the two kinds, and the cycle above is then a compile error to explain); a section

- **Guards on `select` arms, and `Selector` for a set of sources known at run time** (branch
  `select-dynamic`, 2026-11-19). The gap came from the ssh package (branch `pty-forward`,
  `Socket.waitWith`): relaying a tunnel to a local connection, it could not leave out an arm by a
  run-time condition ("watch `local.writable()` only while bytes are pending for it") and spelled
  out twelve selects, one per combination; and nothing could wait on N connections or N tunnels,
  which blocks a multi-connection `ssh -L` and `-R`. The surface is [select](/spec/threads/#select)
  and [selectors](/spec/threads/#selectors).
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19: **any arm but `else` may end in an `if` guard**,
    written as a match arm's is, after the operation and its `as` pattern. **A false guard makes the
    arm absent**: not evaluated beyond its guard, not watched, never run, its value never sent. **The
    guard is evaluated first**, with the arms' other expressions, once and in written order, before
    any arm is tried, so it cannot name the arm's pattern's bindings, which no value has yet. WHY:
    evaluating the guard first lets it protect the arm's own expressions (`conns(i).readable() if i
    < n`) and keeps a value meant for an absent arm from being computed; an arm that is not there
    should cost nothing. ALTERNATIVES: the guard after the arm's expressions (a send's value computed
    for nothing, and a guard that cannot protect its arm); a guard that sees the received value, as
    a match guard sees its bindings (it would have to receive before deciding, then put the value
    back, which a channel cannot do without reordering).
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19: **a select whose every arm is guarded off, with no
    `after` or `else` left, traps**, and so does `wait` on an empty `Selector`. WHY: only a
    cancellation could end such a wait, which is almost always a loop's exit condition gone wrong;
    the trap names it where it happens, instead of a thread that hangs or a deadlock report later.
    A thread meant to wait for its cancellation says so with an `after` or a channel. ALTERNATIVES:
    waiting for cancellation (as the brief offered; silent where it is a bug); a compile-time error
    (guards are run-time values, so it can only be caught at run time).
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19: **`after` takes a guard; `else` does not.** A false
    guard on `after` leaves a select that waits until an arm runs. `else`'s body follows it with no
    arrow, so `else if c then a else b` already means an `if` there. WHY: a guarded `after` is the
    "time out only while something is pending" case; a guarded `else` is `after 0` guarded, which
    already exists. ALTERNATIVES: a guard on `else` (`else if` would read two ways).
  - Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19: **the dynamic form is a library type,
    `avin.threads.Selector[K: Eq]`**: entries `receive(channel, key) -> SelectReceive[T]` (whose
    `received()` holds what was received), `send(channel, x, key)`, `readable(source, key)` and
    `writable(sink, key)`; `remove(key)`, `removeWhere(p)`, `clear()`, `size`, `isEmpty`; waits
    `wait() -> K`, `within(timeout)`, `until(deadline)` and `poll() -> Option[K]`. The entries stay
    between waits; a send entry is taken out once its value has gone. Each entry is the arm object a
    `select` block is read into, and a wait runs the same library loop and the same runtime park on
    the poller, so there is one wait path. WHY: a set of N sources needs a value the program can
    build, keep and change between waits, and keys of the program's choosing answer "which one"
    without index bookkeeping; mixed kinds (channels and streams) live in one set. ALTERNATIVES: a
    `for` arm in `select` (`for c in conns: c.readable() -> …`), which reads well for one homogeneous
    collection but rebuilds the set every time the select is reached, needs a second arm per kind of
    source, and adds a binding form to the select grammar; both (two ways to say the same thing, the
    `for` arm being sugar the library type can carry later if programs want it); entries answered by
    index (indices shift as entries are removed); a send entry that stays after it ran (it would send
    the same value again at the next wait).
    **Review with the user:** the `Selector` surface (its name, keys over indices, `receive`
    answering the entry, a send entry taken out once it ran), and whether `select` should gain a
    `for` arm as sugar over it.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (branch `stdin-readiness`): **`io.stdin()` is a
  `Readiness`, any thread may wait on it, and `readAvailable(max)` reads only what is there.**
  Source: the `stdio-bytes` branch found that the tui package could not move off its own Sysl
  binding of descriptor 0 (`sysl.io.wait.ready` with a time limit, then a raw read), because
  `io.stdin()` had no timed wait and bytes in the runtime's shared buffer would never show as the
  descriptor's readiness; any interactive program (a TUI, a REPL, a language server with timers)
  needs standard input in one wait with channels and timers. Details settled: (1) **Ready** means
  bytes are in the shared buffer (a `readLine`'s read-ahead among them), the input has ended or
  failed, standard input is a file (whose read never waits), or descriptor 0 polls readable;
  `readable()` never waits, and answers `false` while another thread holds the input lock.
  (2) **Ownership: none.** Standard input is process-global, so any thread may name it in a
  select or a `Selector`, and several at once; a connection keeps its owner rule. (3) **The lock**:
  a select never takes `input_readers` to wait. Every select arm on standard input is enlisted on
  a runtime queue (`input_changed`) that every reader notifies as it lets the lock go, so bytes
  another thread's `readLine` left in the buffer end the wait; one select at a time watches
  descriptor 0 on the poller (which holds one waiter per descriptor and direction), and hands the
  watch on, waking the others, when its wait ends; a reader parked on descriptor 0 takes the
  watch's place and tells the selects when it lets go. The library is unchanged: the runtime's
  `select_watch` takes descriptor 0 by this path. (4) **`readAvailable(max) ->
  Result[Option[Array[byte]], IoError]`**: `Some` of what `read(max)` would answer without
  waiting, an empty array at the end, `None` where a read would wait or another thread is
  reading; it is a method of `StandardInputBytes`, not of `Reader`. WHY: one wait path for every
  source; the queue closes the one gap readiness on the descriptor alone leaves (bytes already
  buffered) without polling; `Option` keeps "nothing yet" apart from "ended", which a TUI must
  tell apart. ALTERNATIVES: only the thread that first waits on standard input may wait on it,
  trapping others (a rule a program could not see, for a resource that has no owner); taking the
  input lock to look (a select would then wait behind a thread parked in `readLine`, past its
  `after`); a select re-trying standard input on a timer (`wakeAt`) while another thread reads
  (polling, and a delay); `readAvailable` answering an empty array for both "nothing yet" and the
  end (ambiguous); `readSome`/`readAvailable` on the `Reader` trait (every reader would owe it,
  and files and connections have no use for it yet). tui switched in its branch `stdin-api`.
  **Review with the user:** the name `readAvailable` and its `Option` answer.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (the user asked for the change, branch
  `method-chain`): **a comparison chain's links may call operator methods; a chain is allowed when
  every link yields `bool`.** `lo <= x < hi` with `x`'s type defining `<=` and `<` as methods is one
  chain, as it is for built-in comparisons, and links of methods mix with built-in links, `==` and
  `!=` among them. The chain keeps its meaning: operands are evaluated left to right, each middle
  operand exactly once, and evaluation stops at the first false link. Each link resolves on its own
  left operand's type, so overloads are chosen per link (`t0 < t <= d` calls `Instant < Instant`
  and then `Instant <= Duration`). A link whose method yields anything but `bool` (a query builder's
  `age < 30` yielding a condition) makes the chain an error naming the link, its method and the type
  it yields, and saying to join the comparisons with `&&` or parenthesize one; `a < b` alone still
  yields whatever the method yields. The compiler lowers a method link through the chain's one
  lowering: the checker records the link's resolved call on two unnamed locals, and the chain
  gives them the operands' values it already holds. Why: chains read as the mathematics they
  write, and the house style asks for them wherever possible; the earlier rule's reason, that a
  method may yield anything, is kept exactly where it applies, a link that does not yield `bool`.
  Alternatives weighed: keeping the error (forces `lo <= x && x < hi` on types with methods only);
  allowing any result type and joining links with the result's own `&&` (no single meaning for
  short-circuiting, and a condition builder's `&&` is a method too); desugaring method chains into
  nested `&&` blocks in the checker (a second lowering of chains to keep in step with the first).
  Amends "the arithmetic operators … are free method names" above.

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (built on branch `machine-conditions`): **the choices
  [machines](/spec/packages/#machines) left open in the manifest.**
  - **A feature that does not exist on a machine turns nothing on there**, even when a feature that
    does exist `enables` it: the selection leaves it out, and what only it would turn on stays off.
    A feature that `requires` it is refused there as requiring a feature that is off. WHY: "does not
    exist" means the same whichever way the feature is reached; turning its modules on through
    another feature would make it exist after all. ALTERNATIVES: refusing a feature that enables an
    absent one (makes a cross-machine package spell its enables twice); taking it through `enables`
    anyway (contradicts its `if`).
  - **`targets = []` is refused**; a package builds for at least one target. WHY: an empty list is
    a package nothing can build, and is more likely a slip than an intent. ALTERNATIVES: reading it
    as every target (the opposite of what it says).
  - **Whether a dependency "reaches further" is asked over the dependent's targets where the entry's
    condition holds**, so `lib { …, if = "macos" }` may name a package that builds only for
    `aarch64-macos`. The check runs whatever machine the build is for, against the manifests.
    WHY: an entry the condition leaves out is not in those machines' builds at all.
    ALTERNATIVES: refusing on every target of the dependent (forces `targets` where `if` already says

  - **A whole workspace resolved for a machine is the members that build for it**, so `avin tidy`
    and `avin vendor` of a workspace answer each target with the members that list it. A

    built for Linux alone has nothing to resolve on macOS. ALTERNATIVES: refusing the workspace on
    the machines some member leaves out.
  - **`link-flags` are passed exactly as written, in order, with no flag merged with another**, after
    the flags of `pkg-config` or `link`. WHY: the spec's "as written"; `-framework` repeated before
    two frameworks must stay two pairs. ALTERNATIVES: removing repeats (breaks `-framework` pairs).
  - **`c-linking`'s `static` and `dynamic` may name a C library the machine leaves out**, which does
    nothing there: a library of a package in the build whose `if` does not hold, or,
    `<package>/<library>`, a library of a dependency whose `if` leaves it out, named by the
    dependency's label (its libraries are not read on that machine, so an unqualified name of one is

  - **`--target` is taken by `avin check` alone** for now, reading every manifest as that machine's

  - **A condition's syntax errors** name the condition and what is wrong at the place: a symbol,
    `!` or `(` wanted (at the end or where a character stands), a `(` never closed, or a word
    following a whole condition; symbols are lowercase and `-` belongs to a word, so a target's name

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (branch `bounded-mailbox`): **A mailbox may be bounded,
  given as `spawn(b, mailbox = Bounded(capacity, overflow))`; a `tell` to a full one drops by the
  actor's `Overflow`, and senders that must know or wait use `offer` and `send`.** `data Mailbox` is
  `Unbounded` (the default) or `Bounded(capacity: int, overflow: Overflow)`, `Overflow` being
  `DropNewest` or `DropOldest`; a capacity less than one traps in `spawn`. `tell` keeps its settled
  promise, never waiting and never failing, and drops as the policy says, counted by
  `ref.dropped() -> long`. `offer(m) -> Result[unit, SendError]` never waits and answers `Err(Full)`;
  `send(m)` and `send(m, timeout)` park the sending thread until there is room (a timed one answering
  `Err(TimedOut)`, a timeout of zero or less being `offer`), as a cancellation point that leaves
  nothing in the mailbox, waking with `Err(Ended)` where the actor ends; an actor's `send` to its own
  full mailbox answers `Err(Full)` at once. `SendError` is `Full`, `TimedOut` or `Ended`; `AskError`
  gains `Full`, and an ask of a full mailbox completes with it at once under either policy, dropping
  nothing to make room. What the actor arranged for itself (a watch's notice, a timer's message, a
  piped future's) goes in outside the bound and is never refused, and stop, restart and escalation
  are not messages, so no bound holds them back; a restart keeps the mailbox and its bound; messages a
  stash gives back do not count again. `Router.pool(…, mailbox)` bounds the router's mailbox and each
  routee's at one capacity, and the router waits for room in the routee it chose (`SmallestMailbox`
  only once every routee is full), so a full pool's backpressure reaches the router's own mailbox,
  where the policy and `offer`/`send` act. A bounded mailbox is a queue under a lock, so the oldest
  message may be dropped and senders may wait on a condition; unbounded actors keep the lock-free
  queue and pay nothing. *Why*: the bound is a property of the actor, chosen where it is started, as
  its supervision and executor are; separating the sender's choice (`tell` fire-and-forget, `offer`
  to know, `send` to wait) from the actor's policy keeps `tell`'s settled meaning and gives every
  program its backpressure path (marshal's queues, a pg pool) with no new wait inside `tell`; an ask
  that cannot be delivered answering at once is what `Ended` already does. *Alternatives weighed*:
  a capacity and policy on `Behaviour` or the `actor` declaration (the same actor wants different
  bounds in different places); a third policy that fails the `tell` (`tell` answers nothing, so the
  failure would be a trap in the sender for the receiver's slowness); a `tell` that waits (breaks the
  settled rule, and deadlocks two actors telling each other); `offer` answering a `bool` (cannot tell
  `Full` from `Ended`); `send` as a `Future` (the message would still be delivered after its awaiter
  was cancelled); a dead-letters hook called with each dropped message (needs a typed callback on the
  mailbox and runs user code inside the sender's `tell`; a counter is enough to observe overload);
  counting the actor's own notices against the bound (a full mailbox would lose a watch's notice of

- Settled on the user's delegation 2026-11-19 (branch `target-keys`): **every cache entry names the
  machine it was built for, in its name and in its key**. A toolchain has a `target` (the compiler's
  own machine unless a build names another). Under `units/`, `shims/`, `cunit/` and `csources/` an

  shipped as `share/avin/lib/<target>/libavinrt-<target>-<key>.a`; a program's directory under
  `build/` is `<name>-<target>-<key>`, which holds its executables and its instance cache; the key
  hashed into each entry also holds the target, and an executable's record does too. Without a cache
  directory the compiler's own machine keeps `.avin/build` and another machine uses
  `.avin/build/<target>`. `avin cache info` lists the entries per target and `avin cache clean
  --target <target>` removes one target's. **Existing caches are not carried over**: an old entry has
  no target in its name, so no build finds it (it is never misread), `avin cache info` lists it as
  `untargeted`, and the least-recently-used sweep removes it, so the first build after the upgrade
  rebuilds. *Why*: a cross build, or a prefix shipping archives for two machines, must never reuse an
  object built for the other, and the name makes the target visible to `info` and `clean` without
  opening a file. *Alternatives weighed*: the target in the hash alone (disjoint, but `info` and
  `clean --target` could not tell targets apart); a subdirectory per target in each kind (the sweep
  and `info` count entries one level down, and a directory would become one entry holding every
  object of its target, evicted whole); keeping old names for the compiler's own machine (a
  compatibility rule with no reader once a second machine exists, and the rebuild is one build). The
  `.avin/build` fallback keeps its path for the compiler's own machine so existing programs'
  directories do not move, which is the one place an old entry stays valid, and its executable
  records carry the target so a stale one is rebuilt. `avin clean` removes a program's builds
  for every target there, and each target's directory once it is empty.

  yield `bool`**, and one that does not is "expected bool, found Cond", the same message any
  non-`bool` condition gets; the condition then binds no names, since an `is` test is never the
  operand of a method `!`. **A method `!` takes no argument at all**, a defaulted one included: `!`
  has no binary form, and an `a ! b` reading would be a new infix operator nobody asked for. `~` and
  `+` keep their one-argument overloads for `a ~ b` and `a + b`. **Generic code reaches them through
  a user trait that declares them** (`trait Flip` with `!() -> Self`); there is no core trait for
  them, since no built-in type's `!`, `~` or `+` is anything generic code over user types needs, and
  `Neg` stays the only prefix core trait. **Where the type has no such method the operator keeps its
  meaning**: on a data type or a class `!a`, `~a` and `+a` are the errors they were ("expected bool",
  "`~` needs an integer or a byte", "`+` needs a number"). **The built-in types stay closed**: a
  method `!`, or `~` or `+` taking no argument, on `int`, `real`, `byte`, `char`, `string`, `bool` or
  a tuple, in an extension or a trait's implementation, is an error ("a prefix `!` on bool is the
  language's own…"); `!` is no longer among the reserved method spellings. **Two prefix operators
  written together stay one name** (`!!x` and `-~x` are the existing "a symbol method has no prefix
  form" error), so nesting is written `! !x` and `- ~x`, as the operator-run rule already said.
  *Alternatives weighed*: requiring `bool` from every method `!` (rules out the query builder the
